subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take the opportunity, before the Prime Minister has quitted the chamber to attend
War Appropriation Bill

to other duties, and during the presence 'here of the three ministers of defence, to ask the government if it would state its position with regard to the question of decorations. Upon inquiries which I have made in various directions it has been stated to me on more than one occasion that the government takes its stand on the incident which happened in the House of Commons in 1919. Hon. members will remember that a select committee of the house was appointed to examine into the question of titles and to report. The committee so reported on May 14, 1919, and a debate ensued some days later in which the recommendations of the report were supported by a majority in the 'house-I think the figures were 96 to 43. As a result of the adoption of that report a humble address was presented to his majesty making reference to two points. The suggestion was made, first, that no more titles should be granted to British subjects domiciled in Canada, and, secondly, that in the case of hereditary titles they should lapse at the death of the then holder.
That humble address was duly sent to his majesty, but that was by no means the only content of that report. There was a further paragraph which I should like to read to the house. Immediately after the reference to the address, the suggestion was made that the titles of both "Right Honourable" and "Honourable" be discontinued, but the suggestion did not meet with the approval of the committee. The report then states:
Your committee, however, do not recommend the discontinuance of the practice of awarding military or naval decorations, such as the Victoria Cross, Military Medal, Military Cross, Conspicuous Service Cross and similar decorations to persons in military or naval services of Canada for exceptional valour and devotion to duty.
It seems to me therefore improbable that what I have been informed is correct, that the government takes its stand upon what happened in the House of Commons-not parliament-in 1919.
The question of decorations has been one of some difficulty, but for generations, so far as Great Britain is concerned, recognition of deeds of valour has been accepted almost as a household word. There may be some who think there is but little value in it, but I am sure I am voicing the opinion of members of the fighting services, members of the services which are connected with the fighting

services, yes, and indeed of a large proportion of the population, when I say that a recognition for valour is something far above recognitions of other descriptions. It has the effect of strengthening the morale of the services.
The other day in this house I mentioned my own personal opinion that I am not more than interested as a rule in the manners and customs of public and governmental life in Great Britain. I prefer to be guided by what I consider the points which count with regard to Canadian public life. But there is a difference in this matter. Our sailors, soldiers and airmen are more than allies with those of other dominions; they are brothers. They are so closely associated with them that it would seem to me something in the nature of a common policy that might well be the directing course with regard to this question of decorations.
Just recently the Canadian No. 1 fighting squadron has been fighting with the Royal Air Force squadrons and with Polish squadrons, and as a result of what was accomplished by these various squadrons recommendations for decorations have been made and decorations have been granted not only to pilots but to ground personnel, recognition thus being given to the fact that a plane in the air must be kept in perfectly fit flying condition by those who do good work on the ground. I am told also that recommendations went forward with regard to personnel connected with No. 1 fighting squadron, but decorations were not granted.
It appears to me it would be of very great interest not only to the services in Canada but to the general public if the government would be good enough to make known what policy actuates it in this matter.

speechtext:
Last night I
attempted to adjourn the debate but apparently I was out of order. I made the attempt for the reason that I wished to -be the first speaker to-day, but it has not worked out so well. The only reason I am speaking to-day is that there has been so much misrepresentation with regard to the problems of British Columbia, and that is what I want to correct.
The principal reason for dissension in our war effort is the fact that we as members do not know Canada as we should. I venture to say that at least seventy-five per cent of the members have never had the privilege of visiting British Columbia and the other

War Appropriation Bill
western provinces. That is not good for Canada or for us as members of parliament, and I am taking this opportunity to invite each member to visit the glorious west at the conclusion of this session. I shall write to each member individually in this regard. I have no authority to speak either for the provincial government, for the municipal authorities, boards of trade or any other organization, but I think I can assure hon. members, on their behalf, that we shall give all visitors a true western welcome and I hope *they will let me know how many are coming. All have passes, and most are of Scottish descent, and it would be an excellent chance for hon. members to show their wives what good fellows they are. I suggest that you bring your families with you.
In my opinion, we have not yet put into effect a full war-time effort and in this connection I may refer to the question of shipbuilding. It may sound strange for me to discuss this subject as a rural member, but it was under consideration last night, and; I wish to point out that we in British Columbia have many year-round harbours. Our climate cannot be surpassed, and notwithstanding any information to the contrary that may have been given to the minister, who I regret is not present at the moment, we have between one and two thousand skilled labourers out of work. That is not in the best interests of Canada at a time when the empire is calling for ships and more ships. A short time ago the representatives of the international machinists union, covering railroad employees, approached the Canadian Pacific Railway with the request that the employees of that system be put back upon a six-day week, and the answer given was that to put these men on the six-day week would throw five hundred skilled men out of work. If you are going to throw five hundred skilled1 men out of work in British Columbia or elsewhere by adopting a six-day week, then I say we have plenty of skilled mechanics.
I should like to quote from the Ottawa Journal of March 11, which in an editorial quotes the following Canadian press dispatch:
Ottawa, March 7.- (CP)-The possibility that Canada's war-time cargo boat construction might be doubled was seen to-day by officials of the munitions and supply department.
That is from the Canadian Press. The editorial continues:
Who are these "officials"? And who authorized them, whoever they may be, to give out such an announcement? Such statements, clearly, should come only under the name, and with the authorization and responsibility, of the minister.
The Canadian Press dispatch, enlarging on the statement of the "officials", went on to say:
"At present the dominion is engaged in building 20 cargo boats, and it was understood the authorization for the building of anything up to 20 more has been received within the past few days from Britain."
And further:
"The cargo boats under construction are merchantmen of the ten thousand ton type. . . ."
Hon. members may wonder why I want this in Hansard, but my friends to the left will not wonder so much when they hear the rest:
Are these statements true? We are afraid they are not true. To begin with, the Journal's information is that Canada is not "engaged in building 20 cargo boats"; that no cargo boats are "under construction".
A little further on in the same editorial we find this:
But why not say so? Why instead have some unnamed "officials" putting out information that is inaccurate and misleading? It is precisely this sort of thing that has caused Mr. Howe no end of trouble, and which, in addition, has made for a lot of public confusion. . . .
And further down it says:
. . . although we think it could be strengthened greatly in its efforts by calling in men to its councils outside of mere party lines. . . .
At the outset the editorial says that these officials, these dollar-a-year men-ninety per cent of them Tories-are giving out misleading information, but further down it asks us to bring these same men into a so-called national government. It would be a fine government! The editorial says they give out misleading information, and I want to tell the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) that in my opinion any bottle-necks we have had have been due to that very fact that he has not been given accurate information, certainly not from British Columbia. And this misleading information comes from a group of officials who are responsible to no one.
In this connection I would commend the government for having appointed a committee to investigate war expenditures. This is a very wise decision and will serve to reassure the public. But I would strongly urge upon the Prime Minister that he appoint another small committee consisting of five to seven private members of this house to tour Canada right away and view the different projects now under construction or in operation. The private member is responsible to the public by whom he is elected. When these so-called official experts give the minister misleading information, as they have unquestionably done, and subsequently it is found to be incorrect, they merely resign. If a small
War Appropriation Bill

committee went around and viewed these projects, for example in Hamilton, they could give the people a true picture.
Let me give one instance of the foolish criticism that is prevalent. This criticism came to me from two of the most prominent Liberals in British Columbia, at Liberal headquarters. A certain project was said to have cost 132,000, which if true would be ridiculous. That story was going round the streets of Vancouver, and if anything ever does go round the streets of Victoria it possibly went there. I took it up with the Minister of National Defence, which is what I think any hon. member should do, to check the veracity of such rash statements, and I found that the actual figure was $490. The hon. member for New Westminster heard the story and I am sure that every hon. member from British Columbia heard that it cost $32,000. Things like that do not help Canada's war effort.

speechtext:
Well, I correct myself; Victoria City has at last wakened up.
Much has been said, in connection with our war effort out there, about geographical difficulties. It is possible that shipbuilding costs and some other costs in our war effort may be greater out there owing to our geographical conditions. But offsetting that we have climatic advantages. We have never disputed the fact that some of the air-training camps should be in the east where you have anywhere from one to forty feet of snow for six months in the year. But our main geographic disadvantage is freight rates. As I see it the government under the War Measures Act have it in their power to overcome that disadvantage. As soon as the railroads saw that we were short of ships they increased our freight rates. The board of transport commissioners may have control of freight rates, but when the poor farmer for the first time in ten years began, not to make money, but merely to break even, the government pegged the price of butter. They could just as well peg freight rates.
There is another matter in respect of which the Pacific coast is not under a handicap. It cannot be disputed that we have skilled labour available as well as eighteen thousand unskilled labourers in Vancouver and the surrounding district. We are not in an all-out war effort while there are two thousand skilled and eighteen thousand unskilled labourers without employment in British Columbia.
It has been stated here that we in British Columbia have certain war orders. But we sold approximately as much lumber before;
(Mr. Cruickshank.]
the only difference is that we sold it to the four corners of the earth. Now we are selling it, and correctly so, wherever the war effort requires us to sell. We have heard much about the ten million dollar plant that we are building for Consolidated Smelters at Trail, but before the war we sold those metals, even -to our everlasting shame be it said-to Germany and Japan. But we sold them.
We have men unemployed in British Columbia. We should put them to work. If it is to the advantage of the war effort that the money be all spent in Ontario we are patriotic enough to agree. But our patriotism leads us to the belief that no matter where ships are built they should be built speedily, and when we have shipyards that are not working to capacity we expect the people of Ontario and Nova Scotia to be equally fair in their consideration of us.
We resent strongly the suggestion made yesterday that there are not these unemployed men in British Columbia. I and, I presume, other hon. members from British Columbia receive letters every day from skilled men seeking employment. We get letters every day from our constituents asking why we are not going full-out in our war effort. I believe the government have done excellent work; in my opinion the Minister of Munitions and Supply is the best qualified man in this house to hold the position he does, but at the same time in fairness to the minister I say he has not been properly advised by some of the so-called officials that he has around him. After the last war the United States found that their most expensive luxury was these dollar-a-year men. The labourer in any line is worthy of his hire. The government should pay a little more attention to the advice of members from the various parts of Canada, who know what is going on. I am citing this particular case simply because the minister does not and could not possibly know what has been going on, with these so-called experts advising him.
On January 28, at the Boundary Bay elementary training school under the empire air training scheme, there were from two to four inches of water nearly all over the six hundred acres of that project. On the same day, at five o'clock in the afternoon, three men were engaged in shingling the roof. With five hundred carpenters unemployed in British Columbia, the province which produces ninety per cent of all the shingles made in Canada, only three men were working. That is not good enough. I know of five men from my own riding who went to this school five times to apply for work. They did not go with letters from their member, either; but they

War Appropriation Bill
could not get work, though they were fully qualified carpenters. Is that an all-out effort? Of course it is not.
There is one expression I do not like to hear in connection wtih our war effort; that is, "up to schedule." As I see it, if a particular project is two months ahead of schedule it is our duty and responsibility as members to see that it is brought four months ahead of schedule. Remember, Hitler is not going to run this war on schedule. If we are two months ahead of our schedule let us work until we are four months ahead of it, and we are not in that position when the conditions I have described exist at Boundary Bay, where they have had to lay down three feet of solid gravel, hauled at great expense, in order to permit access to the very cabins where the young aviators are going to live. Is that an all-out effort? I am not blaming the minister for that; no fair-minded person would blame him. He cannot know every detail, but, fortunately or unfortunately, he has to rely upon his experts, ninety per cent of whom are Tories.

speechtext:
I have erred in saying that the resolution was passed unanimously; what I should have said was that the resolution was adopted at that time. When the Liberal administration came into office in 1921 our party considered the matter, and I understood was unanimous in its view that this resolution should govern in the matter of the bestowal of titles and decorations. All the administrations of which I have been head have consistently held the view that the resolution was one passed by the House of Commons, and that until it was amended or rescinded by this house, the government should consider itself bound by the resolution. It is true that when the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett was in office he did not take the same view. He contended that the resolution was passed by only one branch of parliament, and that the resolution of the House of Commons of one parliament did not necessarily bind the Houses of Commons of succeeding parliaments. Nevertheless the view taken by the present administration has been and is that until the resolution respecting titles and decorations adopted by the House of Commons of Canada is amended or rescinded by the House of Commons itself, we should consider ourselves bound by it.
I should add that on one or two occasions motions were presented from the other side of the house to have the resolution reconsidered. Speaking offhand, I cannot recall the years, but, if I am not mistaken, there were two occasions. In one instance Mr. Ladner, one of the members from British Columbia, moved that the house should reconsider the resolution on titles and decorations. At another time Hon. Mr. Cahan brought in a motion asking for the appointment of a committee to consider the whole matter. My recollection is that neither of these motions was entertained by the house, and for that reason, among others, this administration has felt that it was right in believing that the general sense of the House of Commons
War Appropriation Bill

reflecting that of the country was against reopening the question of titles and decorations.
The hon. member for Yale has been careful in his remarks to distinguish between what is involved in the conferring of titles and what is involved in the conferring of decorations. I think he has been wise in so doing. I do not believe there possibly can be in the public mind the same objection to the conferring of decorations that there is to the conferring of knighthoods, which tend to create class distinctions which certain decorations certainly do not. So I shall confine my remarks at the moment, as my hon. friend has, more particularly to the question of decorations.
Decorations fall into two classes; those in the nature of awards for gallantry, the recognition of valour, and those given in recognition of other services. The latter decorations are associated with certain orders of chivalry. As hon. members are no doubt aware, the orders of chivalry have different classes. The orders and classes constitute a sort of hierarchy of recognition. I might illustrate by referring to the Order of St. Michael and St. George. The lowest class of this order is the C.M.G. decoration, companion of the order of St. Michael and St. George. There is next a higher class, the K.C.M.G., which makes the recipient a knight commander of St. Michael and St. George. There is also a still higher class in the order, the G.C.M.G., which makes the recipient a grand commander of the order of St. Michael and St. George. The K.C.M.G. carries with it a right to the title "Sir". The wife of the knight is known as "Lady". There are also in the orders of chivalry the Order of the Bath, the Order of the British Empire, the Royal Victorian Order, and others that do not come to my mind at the moment, and which for the most part are specifically restricted.
What I have said will, I believe, help to illustrate that there is a distinction between decorations belonging to orders of chivalry and decorations belonging to orders of valour.
The awards for the recognition of valour and gallantry are the M.C., the military cross; the D.S.O., the distinguished service order; the D.C.M., the distinguished conduct medal; the M.M., the military medal; the D.F.C., the distinguished flying cross; the D.S.C., the distinguished service cross and, of course, the V.C., the Victoria cross, the most distinguished of all decorations. There may be one or two others which I have not noted.
What I would say to the house in reply to the hon. member's question is that so far as awards for gallantry and recognitions of valour are concerned, this government has
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
never taken any stand against such awards being made. I am glad my hon. friend has raised the question, because I have seen in the press the criticism that the administration has prevented Canadians in the field, who have proven themselves equally as gallant as those of other countries, from receiving recognition. As a matter of fact the government has never thought of in any way depriving members of the fighting forces from any recognition for gallantry, or from receiving any of the decorations I have mentioned as conferred for valour.
So far as the decorations in the orders of chivalry are concerned, we have felt that by the terms of the resolution of this house they were ruled out. As to the others, I can only repeat that I am sure the last thought in the minds not only of members of the government but of all hon. members would be that at this of all times we should deprive any one of any right or privilege of recognition for gallantry or valour, but rather that we would be pleased to see that recognition accorded to anyone who might be recommended for such distinction.

speechtext:
It is not my intention to participate in any lengthy debate with respect to this matter. Certainly I am not going to revive the discussion on titles, or decorations for chivalry. All hon. members have their opinions respecting these matters. Personally I have never been able to understand why a citizen of Canada should be debarred from receiving the same recognition from his sovereign that a citizen of Newfoundland. New Zealand or Australia may obtain. However, that is only by the way.
The point immediately under discussion comes from the suggestion that the government itself or some department of it has laid down a rule whereby no decoration for valour may be given to any member of the Canadian armed forces, except it be for valour in the face of the enemy. I understand that is the distinction which has been put forward. I am very glad to hear from the lips of the Prime Minister this afternoon, if I understood him correctly, that the government has taken no action at all in regard to this matter, and that the position is as it was.

Yes; that is a fair statement and a fair understanding, and I believe it will bring substantial comfort to the men in our forces. The sailor, soldier or airman who has performed a gallant service, whether in the face of the enemy or in some other sphere of his activity, values far more the testimony of his sovereign in the form of

War Appropriation Bill
a decoration than he would a gift of money or anything of that kind. There is a psychological effect in such decorations which more than anything else one could imagine lifts the morale of the fighting forces. I believe it will be a matter of -profound relief to the men in the armed forces when they understand that the position to-day is exactly as it was in previous wars. The Prime Minister's statement has cleared up the point and will allay much of the suspicion, uneasiness and unrest which has developed.
I cannot understand how the question could have arisen unless there was an intimation from some source that the position was to be altered; there must have been some basis for the story. For the moment I am content to allow the matter to rest where it is, on the assumption that the Prime Minister has described the exact position. Had it been otherwise I should have felt it my duty to protest against any change in the matter of granting decorations for valour.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few observations dealing with certain military matters which, I believe, would fall under paragraph (b) of the resolution, which reads:
(b) the conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada.
I should like to deal first with the plan known as the thirty-day training scheme. The Minister of National Defence announced some time ago that this scheme would be changed from a thirty-day scheme to a four months' scheme.
I have no doubt many hon. members have taken the opportunity to inspect first-hand one or several of the thirty-nine training centres at different points across Canada. Any hon. member who has done so will have seen the fine sets of buildings, the nature of the equipment, and the facilities available for the training of troops. These training centres are served by an efficient permanent staff of qualified officers, non-commissioned officers and instructors. It has appeared to me most unfortunate, and possibly something in the nature of a tragedy, that these staffs of qualified officers and men, these facilities which have been set up at the cost of millions of dollars, should have been used only for the training of recruits for a period of some nineteen days for service only in Canada.
My contention is that this highly trained personnel which makes up the permanent staffs at training centres should be used for the training of men in the active forces. It seems unfortunate that such facilities should be available and such sums of money spent only to train men for service in Canada. I hope that in the near future the Minister of
National Defence will make an announcement to the effect that these training centres will be used only for the training of men for overseas service.
Some time ago I asked the Minister of National War Services if the regulations then being revised, and relating to the conduct of these camps, would be submitted to the house for debate. He replied that they would not, and that they would be placed on the table after they were agreed upon.

The point I wish to emphasize is that under the present set-up the regulations will affect anywhere from 100,000 to 200,000 young men. Hon. members will agree that any regulations affecting that number of citizens of Canada are of sufficient importance to warrant being brought into this 'house for debate. Anyone who has taken the time or the trouble to examine the set of regulations issued last fall will find many flaws and defects in them. I shall point out just one. The first regulations provided that at the end of the thirty-day training period the recruit would be attached to a reserve force unit. The recruit was not obliged to continue his training. It is quite true that he was requested to continue his training, but no provision was made for his transportation, nor was he to be paid for the time spent undergoing training. I think everyone will agree that any such regulations are absurd. It must be remembered that the average recruit works during

the day and we can hardly expect him to take training at night without pay and to pay his own transportation costs.
I have noticed in the press that under the new set-up the recruit will be attached to a reserve force unit at the end of the four months period. Whether this will be changed, I do not know. I know of one unit which got 400 recruits from men who trained in the first two classes of October and November, and yet a check-up in February reveals that only six are now taking training. I say again that the men are not to be blamed because they must provide for their own transportation, and they receive no pay. I think I am quite safe in saying that if the 85,000 or 90,000 men who were trained under the first, second and third thirty-day training schemes were called up again for training, they would have to start at the beginning.

I should like to refer to one other matter in connection with this training scheme, namely, the exemptions. I do not know just what exemptions or postponements are going to be allowed), because the rules have not been brought down. Certain statements have been made in the house that postponements will be granted for farmers' sons. Under the present regulations applications for postponement are made in writing to the divisional registrar. A recruit may live from 150 to 200 miles from the point where the divisional registrar is located. I know of many cases where little if any consideration has been given to the applications. I suggest to the minister that in connection with the next training period he consider having these appeals heard by the county judges. It would be a simple matter for a county judge to sit at two or three different places within his jurisdiction and hear the appeals of farmers' sons or any others who wish to apply for exemption. A recruit would thus be given the opportunity of appearing in person. I am satisfied that

if some such arrangement were worked out it would do away with much of the dissatisfaction that exists to-day in connection with the hearing of appeals.
A number of young farmers have been placed in awkward positions because their appeals have received little or no consideration by the registrars. It is difficult for a farmer to get help to-day, and the reason is quite apparent. The average man can come to the city to work and get much higher wages. In the riding which I represent the Ontario hydro have been carrying on a great deal of construction work and men are very scarce. Many of the young men who have been called up for training have suffered real hardship because in some cases they were unable to get proper help to look after their stock. Some of these men were living with elderly or ailing parents and they had milch cows and other stock that needed daily attention. I hope the minister will give some heed to the request that these appeals be heard by the county judges.
Replying yesterday to a question asked in regard to the cost of the training centres, the Minister of National Defence referred the hon. member asking the question to page 908 of Hansard of February 21, 1941, where a statement is set out giving the cost of certain details in connection with the training centres. If they cannot be separated, I shall be quite glad to have them as they can be given. With the information in regard to these eleven items before us we shall be able to get an accurate picture of what the three months' training period has cost to date.
Shortly after the Minister of National Defence returned from England he made an announcement through the press that there would be some increase in the size of our armed forces. But so far these increases have been very small, and I wonder if the minister realizes what a serious damper has been put on the enthusiasm of the youth of this country in their attempts to enlist. Many young men have tried for months and months to join certain branches of the service, but have been unable to do so. Perhaps a very small quota would be called for at a certain depot or for a certain battalion. Many men would travel miles and miles, hitch-hike their way, and on their arrival find that the quota had been
filled. Naturally a man who has had some connection with a military unit is attached to that unit. He has some choice as to the branch of the service he would like to join. I suggest to the minister, having regard to the difficulty of getting recruits at the present time, that if he would seriously consider the question of calling up the reserve force units as active force units and allowing these reserve force units to retain their identity, he would get all the recruits he wants.
With regard to these reserve force units, they were mobilized in June, 1940, at least eight full months ago.

speechtext:
Not "mobilized." My
hon. friend does not mean that. I think my hon. friend gives the impression that they were mobilized for the purposes of overseas service. We use the expression "mobilization" in that connection. They were authorized to recruit up to full strength as reserve units; they were not mobilized.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Quite right; they were
authorized to recruit in June, 1940, and in a a very few weeks those units were up to full strength. All recruitment for reserve force units ceased on the 15th of August, 1940. In the eight months which have passed these units have completed thirty days' training. Of that thirty days fourteen days, or fifteen days in some instances, were put in at a military camp. So that in the remaining seven and a half months these units have trained only fourteen or fifteen days.
Much of this training has been carried out under most discouraging circumstances, on account of lack of training equipment. But the point which I wish to emphasize is that, at this critical juncture, when the time feature is so essential, these units have trained only thirty days in eight months.
What is the reason? Are we still short of training equipment? Surely this is not possible when you consider that we are in the eighteenth month of the war. We are constantly assured by the propaganda agency at Ottawa that we are up to schedule; in fact, the hon. member who spoke a few minutes ago mentioned that certain things were two months ahead of schedule. The Minister of Munitions and Supply loves to talk in this chamber about the output of Bren guns. I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply to explain to the house why active force units are so very short of Bren guns for training purposes; why active force units are short of gas-training equipment, anti-tank guns, grenades, and many other items.
Another point I should like to mention to the Minister of National Defence is the number of very fine armouries in eastern
War Appropriation Bill

Ontario which at the present time are being used only for reserve force units. To quote j ust two: in the town of Picton is one of the finest-equipped armouries in eastern Canada. In 1939 there was quartered in that armoury a complete battalion which is now in England. Yet to-day less than a hundred men are using it, and they belong to a reserve force unit. There are fine armouries at Belleville, Napanee, Trenton, Picton, Madoc, and Norwood, all being used by reserve force units. I hope the Minister of National Defence will announce that in the future these armouries will be used only for active force units.
I well remember being in this house the day the mobilization bill was passed, and how the Prime Minister, in a most pleading voice, stated that he wished that his government had the necessary powers that night to act. Well, in a very short time that bill was passed, and what was the result? From the mobilization bill so far we have this farce of a thirty-day training scheme. It is beyond me how any government with a general staff such as they profess to have at Ottawa, with full knowledge of what is going on overseas, could conceive of and put into execution such an utter farce of a training scheme, calling for only thirty days' training; and now, after months of delay, the scheme is to be changed to provide four months' training. I say to the minister that even four months' training does not meet the needs of this country.
Recently the government had a series of radio talks which they called, " Let's Face the Facts." Why not face the facts right here in this house? Let us as members of parliament show, for once, a little backbone, and face the facts and admit that conscription of all man-power for service anywhere in the world is the only answer to the present situation. Any young Canadian who will not fight for his country is not fit to receive the benefits that this country gives to him. Why is recruiting at the present time so slow? We have to-day two systems; on the one hand a voluntary system, and on the other a half-baked idea of compulsory military training, attempting to work side by side. In addition, this government has seen fit to set trainees in a preferred class. Speaking in this chamber last November, I pointed out to the Minister of National Defence that certain articles were not issued to members of the non-permanent active militia, as they were called at that time. When he replied he stated that I should know that the members of the nonpermanent militia did not receive underwear, socks and other similar articles. But all trainees are members of the reserve forces, and they receive socks, boots and all the rest of it, and in addition, when they leave the

training centre they take their socks, boots, underwear and other articles with them to keep.

No, I cannot say, but it does not matter how much it costs; this country can provide the money for it. Everyone says that these soldiers are heroes and should have the best of everything. They are only here a short time before they go overseas and the one thing that means the most to them is denied. If hon. members want to know the popular reaction let them visit the active force unit in this city. Let them browse around among the men and they will perhaps get some idea of the magnitude of the storm that is brewing at the present time.
Surely the time is long past when this government should dwell, as they do continually, on the result of the last election. We all know that the Liberal party received more votes than any other party in the house. But it is not votes that count to-day; it is bullets, machine guns, tanks, aeroplanes and all the other implements of war.
You expect the finest young men in Canada to enlist, and they are willing to risk their very lives. The government is asking the people to save and to lend every cent. The government is asking the people of Canada to make the supreme war effort. Is it not only fair and just, then, that in the administration and direction of the war effort all shades of political opinion in this dominion should be represented?
I would appeal to the members of this house who are veterans of the last war and who now support the Liberal party. I say to them: You know better than anyone else what war means, because you have seen it with your own eyes. Then take a look around your own riding and investigate the conditions of the reserve force and the active force units. Consider the folly of the thirty-day training scheme we have been following. Inquire as to the shortage of equipment in all units. Investigate the endless red tape that seems to delay and tie up everything that the government controls, and then just think back a few years when you were soldiers in France. Think of some of the days when you were on the Somme, at Ypres, or at

141S

Courcelette, or that Easter morning at Vimy Ridge. In those days we had very definite objectives and those objectives were gained only by careful planning and full cooperation with all branches of the service. At Vimy there was the greatest barrage that had ever taken place up to that time, and yet when we crossed over that ridge we saw the advantage of the barrage because it had paved the way for the victory that followed. Any members of this house who were at Amiens on August 8 will recall the perfect clockwork timing of the whole British army in every detail. The result was that the German army was simply rolled back in utter confusion.
I mention this simply to illustrate the need of unity and complete cooperation of all to win victory. When we were in France every soldier some time or other was in a tight spot. At that time it did not matter very much to the soldier what religion or politics his comrades professed. He did not care whether they were interested in party patronage or in the survival of any political party; if anyone had dared to suggest such a thing to a soldier in France he would have been branded as a traitor to his country. At that time the soldiers in France looked to the government and the people of Canada to bury and forget all such considerations, and to supply them with all needed reinforcements and implements of war. In those days hon. members who were in France saw the need of unity in the country. But great as that need was in 1914-18, to-day the need is far greater. We who are returned soldiers and now elected members of this parliament, which is the only legal constituted authority in this country, have grave responsibilities. Is history to recount that we, the members of this parliament in the year 1941, were more concerned with political patronage, with the survival of our party, and things of this nature; that we placed these things before the urgent need of Britain and the immediate mobilization of all the man-power in Canada for service overseas?

Are you so blind in that province that you cannot see what is coming? Are you concerned only with votes and the result of the next election? I warn the Minister of Justice that his remarks in this house will do more to create distrust and disunity and to hinder the war effort than any remarks made here since the war began.
The cry of conscription is again brought up. Well, your government introduced a measure of conscription, and when the vote was taken every member present in this house, except two, voted for it. I ask the Minister of Justice, who has stated that he speaks for the province of Quebec, and who apparently spoke for the Prime Minister, what he proposes to do in the event of reverses to our forces overseas making it necessary to supply a large number of reinforcements-yes, even to have conscription? Does he intend to continue to bury his head in the sand, or does he intend to face the realities of 1941? Members of this government are quite fond of referring to the number of votes their party polled in the last election, but I notice that they carefully refrain from making any reference to the soldier vote overseas. The soldiers overseas did not approve of the war effort of this government, and I am sure the boys overseas will be highly pleased when they read the remarkable speech of the Minister of Justice. Will that speech convey to them that Canada is united behind them?
I wonder whether this government fully realize what is going to happen when the people of Canada fully apprehend the truth about the muddle in aeroplane production, the truth about the shortage of army equipment after eighteen months at war, the truth about the thirty-day training plan. I warn the Prime Minister and his government that the day of promises is long past; the people of Canada in 1941 want results and not promises. And let the Prime Minister not forget what he has often stated in this house, that the will of the people of Canada is supreme over parliament. When the people of Canada realize the whole truth as to how our war effort has bogged down they will tear your government to pieces, just as Mr. Churchill said the armies of Britain would tear Mussolini's empire to shreds. Let the Prime Minister continue talking about the mandate he received at the last election; let his ministers keep on crying "saboteur" and "fifth columnist" in reply to justified criticism

speechtext:
I had intended this afternoon to put on the record some statements which might be of interest to the committee in connection with this resolution. Contrary to what the leader of the opposition has supposed, I shall not take very much time in replying to the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. White). I propose to make a statement to the committee with regard to some matters relating to the army programme in order that the committee may have that information for consideration and as a basis for asking further questions if they so desire. But as a member of this house I cannot allow to go unnoticed some of the things which my hon. friend has said. I do not propose at the moment to deal with the thirty-day training period; I shall come to that in its proper order.
I do want to say most emphatically, Mr. Chairman, that a member of the house who speaks of unity and the complete cooperation of all, and who delivers himself as the hon. member has this afternoon, to say the least certainly is not entirely consistent, and I am sure that is a very weak phrase. Listening to some speeches in this house, including that of my hon. friend, I have sometimes felt that in this country there are some people who are never satisfied unless they are putting a burr under the saddle or creating some difficulty, instead of endeavouring to cultivate unity. My hon. friend was the follower of a gentleman who pledged that there would be no conscription in Canada; my hon. friend was elected on that platform, yet to-day he rises and speaks about the province of Quebec leading this country. I say to my hon. friend that this is unworthy of a member of this house, and I submit that it is unworthy of a gentleman who wears the king's uniform, as he does at the moment. When the hon. gentleman talks about party patronage I tell him he had better adduce some instances of that patronage in connection with this government's war effort before he talks about it. I invite him at any stage of the game, at any stage of this committee's proceedings, to produce any evidence of party patronage in connection with the administration of military affairs. I shall be happy indeed to examine it very fully.
My hon. friend is an officer, wearing his majesty's uniform. If I may presume to offer the suggestion, one of his duties is to endeavour to see to it that the men under his command, the men who salute him, are given a reasonable amount of consideration
War Appropriation Bill

and are not incited to find fault with their lot. It seems to me that one of the things an officer has to do is to take care of his men and endeavour to give them as much assistance and comfort as possible. My hon. friend knows that the reason we have so many men in these camps in Canada to-day is the fact that, thank God, there have not been casualties overseas, and we have not had to send men over as replacements. Knowing that, when he states that there is a feeling of unrest, that there is absence without leave, that there is distrust and dissatisfaction among the men, and that there is a storm brewing, I submit that he is not doing himself justice, nor do I think he is doing justice to the armed forces of this country.
I suggest to my hon. friend that he and I, and everybody in this house, ought to endeavour to see that these men are as fully satisfied as they can be; but I suggest to him advisedly that I do not think the way to do this is to provide free transportation for a soldier when he wants to go on week-end leave, and I say that very frankly. I believe there are other ways of doing it. Those other ways are to look after our men; to explain to them the situation which exists in this country, instead of endeavouring-as my hon. friend would do-to place some sop before them in the way of free transportation in order that they may be satisfied. If I know the men of this countiy-and I think I know something of them; I had some experience in the last war-they do not want to be coddled. These men are not particularly asking for these things; they just want to know what is going on. It is up to officers such as my hon. friend to explain matters to them instead of talking about distrust, dissatisfaction, unrest, storms brewing, and things of that kind.
I suggest to my hon. friend that we should get down to a discussion of what is before this house, namely this war programme. My hon. friend is perfectly justified, or at least has a perfect right, to say all he wants to say against the training scheme. He has a perfect right to find fault with lack of equipment, if he wants to do so. That is his privilege, if he thinks that is helping in connection with the war effort. He has a perfect right to find fault as he wishes; but to say there is dissatisfaction and unrest when as a matter of fact the men are in Canada instead of overseas because of the fact I have mentioned, the fact that there have not been casualties and they have not been required, is not performing the duty which I think an hon. member should perform in this house.
Now may I deal with some of the matters which have been brought up, and I will deal

with them in the course of what I have to say as to the army programme generally. I feel sure that my hon. friend is sound at heart as a Canadian, but I do not think this talk of party patronage, following an attack on a particular province, comes with very good grace from him. I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he ought to clean his own house before he starts attacking other people.
May I now deal with some of the matters in connection with the army programme in which I hope the committee may be interested. I will deal with the thirty day training plan when I come to that part of my remarks having to do with Canadian activity. My hon. friend referred to the headquarters staff rather slightingly and said that if we had a staff anything like the staff we talk about surely we never would have commenced the thirty-day training scheme, which he called a farce. The staff at national defence headquarters, in whom I have the fullest confidence -and I hope my hon. friend will come to have that confidence also, if he does not have it now-prepared an appreciation of the situation as it existed late last fall, just before we went overseas. In that appreciation they assessed as well as they could the possible eventualities in connection with the need for armed forces. That had to take into account not simply Canada but also the United Kingdom and Europe. In fact the world has become exceedingly small these days, and an appreciation of this kind practically has to cover the globe. That appreciation was not simply the work of the army staff. It was gone over by the chief of the naval staff and the chief of the air staff; it was concurred in by all those officers and submitted to defence council. Defence council went over it and then submitted it to the war committee of the cabinet, together with the measures it was thought should be taken by the navy, the army and the air force in order to prepare as best we could for half a dozen eventualities which might arise.
My hon. friend speaks about Vimy Ridge and the planning at Amiens. I am not contending that we had any such timed planning as that, but I do say we had the best plan that could be devised under the uncertain and unpredictable circumstances which faced us, drawn up by the men best qualified to do this planning. That plan was submitted to the war committee of the cabinet, where it was gone over very carefully. It was approved in principle, but it was thought wise-and I think the country approved-that we should go overseas and consult at first hand with those with whose plans we wanted to integrate ours. As has been said time and again- and it cannot be said too often-at the present

War Appropriation Bill
time our front line is on the English channel, and it was the effort over there with which we were endeavouring to match up. We studied the possibility of other services taking on activities which the army proposed to undertake ; of the army taking on some of the activities which the navy might propose to undertake in connection with coast defence, of the army and navy taking on some of the activities which the air force proposed to undertake. The plan submitted finally was one which was regarded as a balanced plan, not balanced in dollars but balanced, so far as effort and equipment were concerned, among the three services.
Just let me say here that I really fail to understand certain criticism that every service is not matched up on the dollar sign, so far as appropriations are concerned. One might just as well say that the fire brigade and the police force in this town ought to have exactly the same number of dollars. They are two different services. One might as well say that the artillery and the infantry ought to have exactly the same number of dollars.
The minister is asking for an allotment for each service, having regard to the programme which each service has worked out, not alone, but in conjunction with the others, and in coordinated effort, under the war committee of the cabinet-and, as I shall show in a moment, in full consultation with the British authorities-in order that in all three services our effort might be most effective.

speechtext:
That is w'hat the minister had to do, and it represents a balanced programme, having regard to the facilities, having regard to the duties and having regard to the potentialities of the three services.
We went overseas. I have not before given the house or this committee any account of what happened, and perhaps at this time I might be pardoned for indicating, and the
house might be interested in knowing, what was done over there. I went over there accompanied by the chief of general staff, by Colonel Magee and by Captain Malone. We went over there in order, if we possibly could, to clew up-if I may use a sailor's term

our army programme with the army programme over there.
We had the chief of staff's appreciation of what we over here believed would be the possible eventualities and possible happenings in the relatively near future. We had, in addition, our plan which had been approved in principle-that is, measures which we thought should be taken. There was no makeshift about it. These had been approved in principle, and our armed programme was developed on the basis of that appreciation.
Our visit to the United Kingdom was first, to set out what we were doing; second, to see if our programme was in step with their own, and, third, to get their views on how our contribution might be made most effective. What we were bent on attaining was the maximum useful army development in aid of the common cause. To do this required an informed appreciation of what might possibly happen, of when our forces might be needed, or what the likely or possible course of the war might be during the present fiscal year.
As hon. members can understand, a definite knowledge of future events is not given to mankind. That appreciation had to be based on probabilities, and those probabilities were to be deduced from the most up-to-date information we could get, and by making the most intelligent use of it.
I had the privilege, I believe it was on four different occasions, of being received by the British Prime Minister and discussing our problems with him, particularly the larger issues and longer views. Then the first conference was arranged with the three service ministers and their staffs. They met and gave us two hours. During that time not only was there discussion but we were given information as to what their forecasts were, what the possibilities might be, and what they were doing in connection with events which were going on in the world generally and which affected the war. They answered many questions. Our discussions were frank; we hid nothing and they hid nothing, and as a result w'e were able to get a clearer conception of what the job really was.
The second conference we had was with Mr. Eden, who was then Secretary of State for War, and with his staff. There the matter of Canada's participation was fully discussed. We had worked out from the plan which I had mentioned what we thought might be a
War Appropriation Bill

useful contribution, having regard to the information we received with respect to the needs. We were prepared to discuss in detail that contribution, or any modification of it.
Mr. Eden was accompanied by Sir John Dill, the chief of general staff, General Hain-ing and General McCready. We there had a long discussion with regard to Canadian participation, and things we might do. We received a very clear idea what the situation was, and I think almost at that meeting arrived at the conclusions with respect to what might be our most effective contribution.
We had the third meeting with Mr. Eden, and some of his staff, with regard to the formation of a Canadian corps. Then we had a fourth meeting with Captain Margesson, who was the new Secretary of State for War, just after he had assumed the position, particularly in regard to armoured formations, and-

The first conference was with all three services. There were the three service ministers,-Mr. Eden, secretary of state for war, Mr. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, and Sir Archibald Sinclair, the secretary of state for air. In each case there were the staffs. There were Sir Dudley Pound, first sea lord, Sir John Dill, chief of the imperial general staff, and Sir Charles Portal, chief of the air staff, and their staffs.
We had a meeting then with Caiptain Margesson which was most informative and instructive. Then I had two or three discussions, one particularly instructive one with Sir Allan Brooke, commander in chief of the home forces, who, hon. members will recall, was on the Canadian corps staff in the great war. That conference left no doubt in my mind as to the effectiveness of the contribution which we had discussed in the previous conference. We found that our plans were fully in keeping with the views of Sir Allan Brooke, who, I believe, had been present at two of the conferences, but with whom I had the additional conference.

speechtext:
I will be able to announce the programme. We reached a complete agreement as to what would be the most useful and effective army contribution from Canada.
Despite the doubts of the hon. member who has just spoken, we told them our object was a full-out contribution with everything Canada has, and as fast as we could give it. And I want to say, also, that they expressed
[DOT]rMr. Ralston.]
appreciation not only for the Canadian contribution wdiich had already been given, but for what we were about to do. And when we were talking to them, too, we assured them that we did not come in any spirit of giving charity, but in the spirit that Canada was in this war at the side of Great Britain.
The programme which we had submitted involved some adjustments in nature of formations and in timing, but it was admittedly a heavy programme in its demands on production, man-power and economic resources. Having settled tentatively on the programme which our friends over there believed would be of the most help, and would be the greatest contribution Canada could make, I did not wait until I got home to communicate that information in full to the Prime Minister and my colleagues, but I cabled them in advance. The result was that within one week after I returned home the programme was endorsed, and was announced by the Prime Minister of Canada, to the letter. That was the programme which had already been discussed and arranged tentatively and provisionally with our friends overseas.
What was that programme? It involved the dispatch in 1941 of four major groups. Hon. members must realize that men are being sent constantly. A new flight of several thousands of men arrived in England only last week. The group put on the priority list to be dispatched in 1941 was the balance of the troops for the Canadian corps. I cannot give hon. members all the details, but I can say to-day that we have in mind a definite arrangement as to the probable occasion on which the movement of these various formations will take place. Hon. members will understand that 1 am not in a position to give that to the house and the public.
The movement of the third division was discussed also and we agreed on the principles governing the timing of the movement of that division. We had the frankest exchange of opinion with regard to the United Kingdom equipment position and our own. We both sat down to work out a definite date or at least a definite date to be worked to on certain principles which we both understood and which have been agreed upon. I think it is clear that we will not equip the third division in whole from this side; I am speaking particularly of field artillery. This for reasons which will perhaps appear obvious to the committee, but of which I cannot give further details other than to say that the third division will be equipped.
I was present with the Prime Minister, Mr. Churchill, at a meeting with Sir Andrew Duncan, Minister of Munitions, General McCready and other staff officers in connection with equipment, and I was given the

War Appropriation Bill
benefit of a good deal of information respecting just what their equipment position is. There are certain understandings with regard to equipment which we both regard as satisfactory.

Yes, with regard to equipment. Then with regard to the army tank brigade, the committee may be interested in knowing just what that formation consists of. I do not propose to give it in detail, for reasons which hon. members will understand. The army tank brigade is often confused in the public mind with the armoured brigade corps. The army tank brigade is a formation which we hope will be working with the Canadian corps. It is an armoured formation which works with the infantry and is an adjunct or supplement to these forces.
There are three tank battalions in the brigade. This formation was strongly recommended by the general officer commanding the Canadian corps and by the chief of the general staff as well. We have a joint arrangement with regard to equipment which I am sure will be satisfactory from the point of view of both sides. There is provision in the estimates for certain portions of the issue of equipment which is being communicated to our friends on the other side. This army tank brigade should prove most valuable to the Canadian corps.
Perhaps hon. members would be interested in knowing what units go to make up this brigade. The leader of the opposition has suggested that as far as possible information should be given in committee. One tank battalion will be made up of the Ontario regiment; another tank battalion will be made up of the Three Rivers regiment and another will be made up of the Calgary regiment. Then there are nine other detachments or sections:
First, 1st Army Tank Brigade Company, RCASC, made up of the 2nd Reserve Corps Troops Company, RCASC, Calgary.
Second, No. 2 Light Field Ambulance, RCAMC, made up from No. 2 Field Ambulance, Toronto.
Third, 1st Army Tank Brigade Workshop, RCOC, made up from No. 3 Reserve Army Field Workshop, Montreal.
Fourth, 1st Army Tank Brigade Ordnance Field Park, RCOC, made up from No. 1 Reserve Ordnance Store Company, Ottawa.
Fifth, No. 59 Light Aid Detachment, RCOC, made up from No. 3 Reserve Army Field Workshop, RCOC, Montreal.
Sixth, No. 60 Light Aid Detachment, RCOC, made up of No. 3 Reserve Army Field Workshop, Montreal.
Seventh, No. 61 Light Aid Detachment, RCOC, made up of No. 3 Reserve Army Field Workshop, RCOC, Montreal.
Eighth, Intelligence Section.
Ninth, Signals Section.
That is expected to be the formation of the army tank brigade.
