That is right. Now comes the armoured division which, as I say, is a vastly different thing. Hon. members will recall that last fall there was mention of forming an armoured corps. There was actually organized an armoured brigade group, which was one unit of that corps. In order that hon. members may have the terminology clearly in their minds, I may say that an armoured division consists of three brigade groups. As I say, last fall an armoured brigade group was formed. Hon. members will recall that it trained under Colonel Worthington at Camp Borden, using in part the tanks which had been obtained from the United States.
We are now forming an armoured division as a whole. This will consist of something like forty units, including signals, engineers, ordnance and all the rest. There will probably
War Appropriation Bill

be about 13,000 personnel. The same arrangement exists with regard to equipment. We have in mind a definite period during which that formation will be in Canada. There is a pretty good idea, as things stand now, as to when it is desired that it should go overseas. The arrangement with regard to equipment is quite satisfactoiy to both sides, and also the arrangement as to when it is likely to be in the field. This formation differs from the army tank brigade. It will be an armoured division which will work on its own and which will be equipped with cruiser tanks. These tanks have been mentioned in the house from time to time by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply. The army tank brigade, on the other hand, is equipped primarily with infantry tanks, the mark III tanks which have been talked about. This unit is regarded as most desirable by our friends over there, and they expressed themselves as extremely gratified that we were able to make the arrangement which was made.
I do not wish to take up unduly the time of the committee, but one has to make the statement some time, and perhaps now is as good a time as any, because I am sure hon. members will be wondering whether their particular units are incorporated in the formation. I shall not mention all the units.
As I said a moment ago, there are three brigade groups. In the first brigade group, it is expected that Lord Strathcona's Horse will be one of the armoured regiments. Another will be the 1st Canadian Cavalry Regiment; another (the 3rd Armoured Regiment) will be the Fort Garry Horse. Another unit (the motor battalion) will be the Westminster Regiment.
In another armoured brigade group will be, it is expected, the 2nd Canadian Motorcycle Regiment, the 4th Canadian Motorcycle Regiment, the 5th Canadian Motorcycle Regiment, and the Perth Regiment. Just to give the locations: Lord Strathcona's Horse is at Listowel, Ontario; the 1st Canadian Cavalry Regiment and the Fort Garry Horse are at Camp Borden; the Westminster Regiment is at Vancouver; the 2nd Canadian Motorcycle Regiment, at Toronto; the 4th Canadian Motorcycle Regiment, at Sussex; the 5th Canadian Motorcycle Regiment, at Esquimalt; the Perth Regiment, at Hamilton.
In the third brigade group will be included the Cape Breton Highlanders, now at. Saint John; the Royal Canadian Artillery, at Petawawa; and another unit, the selection of which has not yet been made; the 41st Light Anti-Aircraft Battery, at Petawawa; the 47th Light Anti-Aircraft Battery at Kingston, and the 87th Light Anti-Aircraft Battery, at Woodstock.

I have here two more sheets of-I was going to say, details, but they are much more than details, of anti-tank batteries, engineers, signals, field ambulances, army service corps, armoured workshops, ordnance field park, field security section, provost company, bath unit, divisional salvage unit, and divisional postal unit. This is the composition of the armoured division.
That was the programme which was arranged with our friends over there; which, as I say, involves an extremely heavy contribution in equipment, in men, and economically, and which was announced by the Prime Minister a short time after we returned home.
If the committee does not mind, I will digress for a minute to complete my remarks with regard to our overseas trip. We had other tasks over there. One, perhaps the most important and certainly to me the most pleasurable, was the visit to our troops, to see them in training, to watch them in operation, and to meet the officers. Another occupation consisted of visits and conferences, some of which I have described, with members of the government, officials of the war office, and representatives of the services, to ascertain the present position and future plans and tell them of our effort and see whether we could help, and to get an appreciation of the battle of Britain so far. I may add that my colleagues entrusted me with a number of special errands for their particular services which I endeavoured to carry out.
With regard to the troops, I have already mentioned to the people of Canada the very happy experience which I had. I spent four days visiting the Canadian troops. The first day I was with the corps troops, the second day with the first division, the third day with the second division, and the fourth day was with the holding units. I will not take the time of the committee to describe my experiences in any detail, but I wish the members of the committee could have shared in some of them. Naturally it was an attractive and interesting thing to see the troops at work, in training on the roads, in billets, and elsewhere in connection with operations._ I saw our mechanical transport, the reconnaissance squadrons flying past at top speed, the field park companies on the roads with their bridging gear and that sort of thing, the units-in one place, it may be, in the trees, in another place out on a broad field-doing their training. I met many old friends and made new ones. It was naturally an exhilarating experience.
I watched the tunnelling company at work, and the so-called "pipe pushers" operating their special apparatus. I saw two fine French-Canadian units on the same afternoon, on

War Appropriation Bill
separate parade grounds, along with the French-Canadian brigadier who is in command, as I remember, of the Calgary Highlanders, the Regiment de Maisonneuve, and the Black Watch. I saw the Canadian Engineers, who have done such an excellent piece of work in building a by-pass road in order to relieve traffic congestion and particularly for the purpose of providing for future operational contingencies. I saw the ammunition and petrol companies on their different grounds and at their particular jobs, with their motor vehicles and transport. Naturally I had a soft spot in my heart for the infantry units of the various brigades, some of whom I saw actually on parade, others-most of them- doing their training. I had an opportunity to ride around one training ground on a universal gun carrier in order to visit all the different training operations which were going on with that battalion, scattered over a field which was probably three-quarters of a mile each way. Also the medical units struck me as particularly efficient. Altogether, the show was one which would have gladdened the heart of any Canadian.
The men over there realize the seriousness of the job ahead of them. As I told the people of Canada a while ago, our men are not over there on any adventure. Always they are looking three ways. Whatever their immediate occupation, whether it be training or marching, or perhaps some recreation, they are looking at the sky and they are looking at the coast. The training experience which I and my hon. friend who preceded me had in the old days, of being on a parade ground without fear of any interference by sea or land, is entirely different from the conditions of to-day.
We may well be proud of the men who compose our armed forces, who to-day are holding the front line in the battle of Britain. I brought from them greetings to their friends in Canada. They are determined to see the job through. They know that the time of trial may come at any time, and they are on their toes, prepared to meet it. If anywhere one could sense the slightest disappointment or any sign of downheartedness, it was because they have not so far been able to get to grips with the enemy, but they realize that the time will not be much longer delayed.
I had of course the pleasure of meeting General McNaughton and the divisional commanders, and of being with them. What I said in that regard to the people of Canada I want to underline here; that is, that no country can be more favoured than Canada in the character of the representatives which we have in our high army command overseas. General McNaughton, General Odium, General
Pearkes, and the brigadiers and battalion commanders and the others right down to the junior officers, are men we can trust and rely upon, men in whose care the honour and glory of Canada and the cause of democracy in the world are, in my humble opinion, entirely safe.
I did see at the same time the repiesenta-tives of the air force. I had the good fortune to meet the officers of the first fighter squadron the first day I was there-not in London but in another town-and naturally one could not help being struck with the appearance of these clean, fine looking young men who were just at that moment out on rest but who had done their full share in defending England against the Hun and in bringing down boche planes in numbers out of proportion to their own.
I did not see the second fighter squadron, although I should have liked to. I also had the pleasure of seeing three out of four commanders of the destroyers over there. Theirs is a job, the greatness of which I think people do not fully realize, that is being done for Canada and for the empire. I talked with three of these }'oung men. There is nothing spectacular about their work. They are out three or four days each way, exposed to wave and wind and cold, with submarines under and enemy planes over, out with one convoy and back in with another. They were in fine heart. They realized that they were doing an important job, and I think the silent service is entitled to a particular word of credit and of commendation for the splendid work which is being carried on.
I did not intend to take up so much time with a recital to the committee of what took place overseas. There were some other matters which I dealt with and in which perhaps the committee will be interested, because they have to do particularly with army activities. There is, for example, the matter of exchange of officers. Perhaps the committee does not know that we have arrangements for exchanges of officers between our Canadian forces overseas and Canada in order that Canadian officers may go overseas to get experience and officers from there may come back to this country and give us the benefit of what they have learned overseas. The other day someone was complaining about our training not being in line with Canadian corps training. We had overseas for two months the director of military training who visited all the formations and got into touch with the training staff, obtaining the best and most thorough information he could as to requirements, so that this might be translated into action when he came back.
Some of the things to which my hon. friend has referred-the four-month training and the

War Appropriation Bill

matter of training officers, for example-are the results of visits of the director of military training at that time, followed by what my associates and I learned while there. We have a staff school overseas, and as soon as the young men who are at that staff school have finished their training we propose to move the school back to Canada in order that young men here may be trained for staff work which will be necessary overseas. In that same connection, in the programme which I have, and which I am placing before the committee, with regard to training, there is provision for the training of between four and six thousand new officers in the coming year at the officers training centre. There will be quite a number of staff officers who will be needed.
At the same time we had the deputy master-general of the ordnance over there to go fully into the question of the provision of motor vehicles, design, the use of them, convenience, how they were standing up, and so on, and he went around seeing the different units and making his examinations with a view to ensuring the very best service that can be given from this side.
I saw the forestry corps; I saw the tunnelling companies, and I also visited the First Lord of the Admiralty in connection with some errands which my colleague the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) had asked me to take on, and particularly in connection with what the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) mentioned last night, namely, the provision of personnel to assist in starting destroyer construction in this country. I had many jobs and made many visits at the air ministry in connection with a number of matters, one particularly being the identification of pilots under the air training scheme. Special matters were discussed, many items of supply. Those were considered before my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply arrived, and after he got there I was happy to hand these things over to him.
We had several opportunities, in connection with air matters, of meeting Lord Beaver-brook and attending the experimental stations where aircraft are tested and tried out, where aircraft are adjusted, where research is done, and of learning of the aircraft supply over there and the development of new types of machines.
I really did not intend to take so long, but that is just a brief resumd in a conversational way of what was done overseas. I came back with this programme to which I have referred, feeling that it was a programme which our friends over there desire to see put

into effect. On this side, I do not propose to go into details, in numbers or anything of that kind. Hon. members know that if we really had a bird's-eye view of Canada we should see this country literally seething with military activity from Halifax to Vancouver. As hon. members know, there are district activities. I had the pleasure only a few weeks ago of having in the district officers commanding in order that we might give them the benefit of what we had learned overseas and that they might understand our plans and have their district activities integrated with those at headquarters. We have camps from Nova Scotia to British Columbia, at Sussex, Aldershot, Valcartier, Petawawa, Barriefield, Borden, Shilo, Dundurn, Sarcee, Nanaimo and other places which perhaps I have missed. In all these camps military activities are going on, where men who would like to get overseas and into this war are stationed for the present, unable to go because of the fact that the situation over there has assumed the static position it has up to the present time.
We have, as hon. members know, coastal defence units, security guards, guards at internment camps and guards at vulnerable points. We are inaugurating in Canada a system of training both for military and for trades vocations which I feel sure will be of undoubted advantage.
That brings me to what my hon. friend has mentioned with regard to recruiting. If my hon. friend is sincere-and I accept his sincerity fully with regard to the matter of recruiting-he will realize that recruiting in Canada at the present time is not the most glamorous affair, not anything like recruiting in the last war. In the last war we had battalions which prominent men in various communities were authorized to raise, and a recruiting campaign was put on. I happened to be a member of a unit which was recruited in that way, with an extremely fine commanding officer. A brigade was recruited with all the glamour and fanfare of a recruiting campaign and an evangelistic meeting. But the situation was that when we got overseas, three battalions of the brigade which had been recruited with all that fanfare and who had been promised that the boys would eat and sleep and fight together, were broken up to form reinforcements of other battalions. This was necessary because of the military situation.
While wre may not have the same glamour in connection with recruiting that we had last time, this is not by any means a glamourous war. I do not know anything that is more grim, more drab than the people of Great Britain having to sit down as they do

War Appropriation Bill
night after night with bombers flying over them and without being able effectively to strike back, waiting for the time when they may be able to join issue. We in Canada should be thankful that the situation is as it is, that we are comparatively safe, that we have freedom of action, that we are able to train without all these difficulties which the men overseas have. I ask my hon. friend who spoke last and talked about men having distrust and suspicion and unrest and all that sort of thing, to preach the doctrine of trust and content and determination to prepare and to serve this country when the time comes.
In this matter of recruiting which my hon. friend has stressed, because he is, I think, a member of a reserve unit himself, and this matter of reserve units, does he realize that we have to-day in Canada no fewer than
175,000	men in reserve units, in addition to over 200,000 that we have in the active service forces? I have made it plain to this committee time and time again that we have not all the equipment we want; does he think that at this time we could possibly equip and train all these units? I ask him to give the staff at national headquarters credit for doing a little planning. What we are endeavouring to do at the present time is to put first things first. We have an active service force recruited in Canada, and we have many who would like to go overseas but are not able to go yet. We have these reserve units.
My hon. friend says he does not like the way in which recruiting is being done. If he is a true member of a reserve unit and trying to do his duty as a Canadian, let me say that reserve units have two roles. One is that if they happen to have a first battalion mobilized overseas-I do not know whether his unit has or not-their first role is to provide recruits as wanted to fill up the ranks of that battalion. The time may come-God forbid that it shall-when that unit may have all it can do to do so, if the battle of Britain strikes as we think it may. Their second role is to do their share in providing the number of recruits which is asked for or allotted to the particular district in which the reserve unit is, to ask these men if they want to enlist, to enlist them and send them to join their battalion.
It is a wonderful thing to be able to go over with your own unit if you can; I know how it broke our hearts to have the Highland brigade broken up, but it had to be. We are in this war to win it, and the only way is by trained man-power equipped with weapons, and with some planning being done. We cannot possibly mobilize 175,000 men in units and send them overseas. I know what the needs are overseas, I know what is told me by 14873-914
the staff there, and I am giving the committee the programme as it is given to me. I say to my hon. friend, his job in a reserve unit is to see that their active unit, if they have one, is kept up to strength; second, to furnish its share of the quota of recruits which may be asked for at any time from the particular district, and, third, to keep his unit in as good shape as he can, so that if the time does come when it is needed as a unit it may be mobilized just as these other units that I have mentioned this afternoon. That is not a job that should make anyone in a reserve unit downcast. I grant it is not spectacular; it means hard work, but no man in a reserve unit need get discouraged and go home and say he does not want to train any more. I know men who are training now and have been for eighteen months and do not know whether they will ever get overseas, but they believe that this job is bigger than the individual, and bigger than the battalion, and they will do what they are told is the best to do in order that our cause may be successful.
That is the situation with regard to recruiting. A call may come for recruits. My colleague the Minister of National Defence for Air needs a number; as I have said, probably between forty thousand and eighty thousand may be needed for the army this year; but many will not be raised by mobilizing battalions, many will have to be raised by the reserve units in numbers as may be required from time to time by battalions which are already mobilized, or new formations. I say to my hon. friend and every hon. member-because there are a good many hon. members who have come to me with regard to reserve units in their constituencies which would like to be mobilized as a whole-there is no man in this house who knows better or realizes more sincerely than I the value of esprit de corps. I know what it means in a unit, and I know what it is to have it broken. At the same time, when that esprit de corps was broken by having the unit broken up we did not sit down and suck our thumbs, we went to work and endeavoured to help build an army out of what was left. I know that my hon. friend's unit and every other unit will do the same. As far as military exigencies will permit I will do everything I can to see that a unit is mobilized as a whole rather than simply sent as reinforcements. More than that I cannot say, and hon. members would not expect me to say more.
That recruiting method, while it may seem drab and unspectacular, is the only method we can adopt at the present time having regard to the demands on our man-power in this country. The reserve units of this

country have been recognized as they never were before, are being mobilized many of them as a whole or made the back-bone of our recruiting organization, and I believe the reserve units will respond to the call to maintain that role and do their very best in whatever capacity they may be called upon to help win this war. That is the true spirit of patriotism, and that is the spirit of these reserve units which we used to call the nonpermanent active militia.
Now a word regarding training activities in Canada. My hon. friend referred to the "farce" of the thirty-day training plan. I take issue with my hon. friend. I believe there have been some valuable lessons learned in connection with that plan. I believe as a whole the training camps have been extremely useful in teaching men their responsibilities as citizens. We have had ninety thousand men, many of whom probably did not think of going into military life at all but who have had an opportunity to see what a military camp is like and have had training of an intensive kind. My hon. friend referred, I think, to only twenty-two days' training; he may be a little off in that connection-

Let us see. I suppose
he will admit they would not train on Sundays; so take away four Sundays. Then there are four Saturday afternoons; I do not know whether he wanted them to train Saturday afternoons. That is two more days off. On Saturday afternoons they had recreation. There was also a day in and a day out. That is why there are twenty-two days of actual training. I say to my hon. friend, to any man in this house and to any man in Canada who knows anything about military training, that this twenty-two days of training was the most intensive and the best twenty-two days of practical training we have had in this country since confederation. I know there are some hon. members on the other side who will agree with that. I have no hesitation in saying that it was a training scheme splendidly conceived and splendidly worked out. There was no opportunity for men just to go to camp and do nothing. Those camps were places where they went and worked hard, improving themselves physically, learning something of the spirit of discipline which should pervade a military camp. That is good for citizenship and good in after life. We have had the benefit of that in connection with those ninety thousand men.
Already it has been said that the thirty-day training was all we could give, but we did not turn down the plan and do nothing because we could give only thirty days. We

did the thirty days training, and did it well. I have no apology whatever to make in connection with the thirty days training; I think it has been a remarkable success. I want here to publicly congratulate the officers who had charge of working out the syllabus, the officers at the camps who so efficiently carried it out, the staff who were able to put up the buildings in the short time available, and those who planned and procured clothing, equipment and rations. These thirty-nine camps were started only in the late summer, and they had to be ready for October in order to get on with the plan.
That was the thirty-day training plan. I am not going to say more about it. I had some other points with regard to it, but I am not going to take up the time of the committee with them just now. Let me go on to what we have planned. I said we were planning for four months training. I said one of the things I had to do overseas was to ascertain the situation over there with regard to training. When I got over there I went into this matter of training thoroughly; and contrary, to what some people and some newspapers have said, that training at military training centres is regarded as the greatest development in this war as far as training is concerned. There has been a great deal of talk about why these men did not train with their units, that it was so much better for men to train together. The point is that you have to give a man a certain amount of physical training, a certain amount of discipline, a certain amount of the rudiments of soldiering, before he is able to work in a formation at all; and with all due respect to the officers of the various units, who have given freely of their time, they have not the opportunity to do the intensive work that is done by the men who for the time being are put on the permanent staff, taken outside of Ottawa to the Connaught ranges and given special courses and special instructions, who are given a syllabus which must be rigidly lived up to, and who are provided with instructors who know their jobs. That is what makes the thirty-day training scheme; that is what makes the value of military training centres as compared with training in units. I can say to the committee that I have the highest military authority for stating that training in training centres far surpasses training in units for elementary and basic work. That is why the thirty-day training was done in that way. That is the way in which basic training is done in England, and that is the way in which it is being done in the United States at the present time, in order that they may get the most for their money in the shortest possible time.

Let me go back to the thirty-day training for a moment and put on record what I have with regard to the usefulness of this scheme. Apart from racial, religious, economic, occupational and language differences between the young men of this country, I would divide them into two main groups:
(a)	Those who have not had the opportunity of belonging to a unit, navy, army or air, in peace time either by reason of the exigencies of schooling or occupation, or by reason of their geographical position;
(b)	Those who may have had an opportunity for military service but who have had no family connection with military life, therefore know nothing about it, and would be naturally hesitant to take part in something which must necessarily be foreign to their normal life.
The thirty-days' training has produced the following results:
(a)	Young men of the first group have had an opportunity to undergo military training and are now enrolled in reserve units. In many instances, individuals who live in small towns and villages and in the country have, upon returning from training centres, organized classes unofficially in their own localities; physical training, shooting, and drill, based upon the instruction they themselves have received;
(b)	Young men of the second category have learned the camaraderie and the interest of military life, and that service of one form or another is incumbent upon the individual in time of war.
War Appropriation Bill

(c)	Training centres have impressed recruits with their individual responsibility to serve whether their service is in agriculture, the armed forces or in business. (d)	Young men of widely differing religious, racial and economic groups have lived, worked and played together for a month and they learned that "the other fellow is really a very good lad." An experience such as this cannot fail to have a lasting effect upon each recruit.
The standard of training laid down to be achieved by each recruit is one which has been highly beneficial, from the point of view of both physical training and discipline. I do not know whether the -hon. member who preceded me referred to the fact that young men have returned home from training centres and organized physical training, shooting and military drill based upon the instructions they themselves received. speechtext:
The debate so far has almost covered the universe. We have discussed more than anything else, perhaps, the Department of Munitions and Supply and the Department of National Defence. I am wondering whether we might not get back to "the more weighty matters" of the resolution.
The resolution stands in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), and primarily, I believe, involves his department. For that reason I d.o not think the resolution should pass without the minister answering one or two questions which to my mind are important.
We are asked to vote authority to raise by way of loan an amount which somebody said the other day was almost equal to the entire debt of Canada since confederation. The resolution calls for the borrowing this year of the tidy sum of $1,300,000,000. Whenever I write that figure down in my notes I do not know where -to stop writing the noughts; I I have to go back and count them all to see if I have inserted enough of them. Our national debt for this young country, with the population of only around 12,000,000 people, has begun to reach figures of an astronomical proportion, and it is doing so without much hope, if any, of this country ever paying off its debt. The other day I did a little browsing in the year book, and I discovered that at the end of the last war our debt stood at $1,191,884,062.50. At the beginning of this war our national debt stood at $3,101,667,570.25, which is an increase in the debt in peace time, between the close of the last war and the beginning of this, to the tune of $2,009,783,507.75. During these twenty years of peace we paid interest on the first great war debt, and during that period we had thirteen years of deficit and seven years of surpluses. I think the minister will have to admit that he has departed from his pay-as-you-go policy.
With regard to paying off this debt, it must be realized, I think, that the time will come when this vast debt will have to be paid off. If we could not at least reduce our debt during years of peace and, in part, of prosperity, how on earth shall we be able to do so if t'he debt grows even higher, and that by leaps and bounds? The minister should tell the committee and the country exactly how he proposes to pay off this debt when the war is over. I ask this question in all honesty because I have been asked the same question myself, and I must confess that by orthodox methods; under our present financial policy I am stuck for an answer.

We have adopted the course of locating these two centres at Victoria and Brockville. The plan of locating them at these two centres is adopted for the following reasons. It gives more centralized control of training, administration and the flow of officer reinforcements. It gives greater uniformity of officer selection and centralized control over the standards required for a commission. We have training centres from Aldershot to Nanaimo, and hon. members will see that naturally there would be some difference in standards at different places. As a matter of fact, one of the hon. members of this committee the other day mentioned to me what I thought was a glaring case of lack of uniformity in connection with the setting and marking of officers' examination papers, which gives rise to dissatisfaction and does not promote efficiency.
Another reason was the uniformity of training and of instruction generally. What seemed desirable was the logical division of an officer's education into (1) experience in discipline and being led; (2) general academic and practical education in those subjects required of all officers, and (3) specialization. Another reason was that staffs can be more carefully selected and trained having regard to their special aptitude for officer's duties if you have them at two officer training centres instead of perhaps thirty-nine or even half that number.

Another reason is that candidates will gain experience by mingling, studying and working with junior officers of all other arms of the service; that is to say, artillery officers, infantry officers and officers of other arms who all go to these officer training centres for the purpose of getting their basic training.
I could give the committee a statement of how an officer qualifies. For the active force an officer has to be in the ranks for four months. Having been in the ranks, if he is considered suitable officer material he is recommended by his commanding officer to take a course at the officers training centre. In that way he is on the road from a cadet to a second lieutenant.

speechtext:
Seniority is a factor; that is as far as I should like to go. From lieutenant to captain is by selection. Then, from captain to major there is a three months' course at an advanced training centre or the Royal Military College. I believe hon. members know that we are using the Royal Military College for the purpose of giving these advanced courses to the more senior officers. We are making that an advanced training centre. From major to lieutenant-colonel there is another three months' course at the Royal Military College. All this is for the active service force.
I was asked about the officers qualifying for the reserve force. The person wishing so to qualify has two alternatives. Under alternative A, he serves the first period in the ranks. He serves in the ranks for one year. He really serves about thirty days; that is to say, if he goes to camp. But that thirty days' training counts on his service for the first step.
Then he takes a course and examination on subjects common to all arms. By taking the course for the officers training corps, his thirty days' training is concurrent. Then he may be recommended as a cadet. On his trip from cadet to the rank of second lieutenant he goes to the officers training centre, and is there for six weeks, taking a course in organization tactics and equipment, et cetera, in the arm which he has selected.
From the rank of second lieutenant to lieutenant he is at the officers training centre for two weeks, taking platoon or equivalent tactics. Then from lieutenant to captain is done by selection, and by attachment to the advanced training centre, if that is practicable, for a period, the length of which depends upon the arm of the service to which he belongs.
I now turn to alternative B. I mention these alternatives now, because the information may be useful to hon. members, and perhaps to officers as well. Under alternative B he is in the ranks for one year, and does training for thirty days. He takes a course and examination common to all arms, and a special examination respecting his own arm of the service. Then, to go from cadet to second lieutenant he spends two weeks in the officers training centre. Then he goes from second lieutenant to lieutenant, under the provisions of K.R. and O. In the examination from lieutenant to captain he takes an examination on subjects common to all arms, and also in subjects special to his own arm, and takes a two weeks' course at the officers training centre or advanced training centre.
Then, from captain to major he goes to an officers training centre or advanced training

centre, and from major to lieutenant-colonel he goes to the Royal Military College for four weeks. I could put on record the present system. The leader of the opposition asked me once before, I believe it was last year, respecting the present method of qualification of officers. I have in my hand a long statement with regard to that matter. I do not, however, think it would be useful at this time because this replaces it.

I should like to give the committee a statement with regard to the alternatives. Possibly I could put on record something which would be useful to officers in the reserve. Reasons are given here why the first alternative I suggested may be preferable. The member of the reserve force who elects to qualify under the first alternative method, for the rank of lieutenant, may follow the same course as for the active force second lieutenant, if he intends to join the force at once; or, if for personal reasons he wishes to spread his qualification over a longer period, he may do so in this way: For the first four weeks at local headquarters, passing an examination, the standard of which would be such as to ensure that those who qualified would be capable of taking up work at the officers training centre at the end of the fifth week. The remainder of the course can be taken in two parts, one of six weeks and one of two weeks, both at an officers training centre. At the conclusion of this he would be qualified as a second lieutenant in the active force. Then it goes on to show the advantage of taking the first alternative for the rank of captain and the rank of major.

4,000	and 6,000 officers will be handled this year, having regard to the formations to which I referred this afternoon, and to the probable reinforcements which will be needed. Therefore hon. members will see that these officers training centres will be busy this year.
Members of the committee would perhaps be interested to know that there will be some necessity for construction. The turning of the reserve training centre at Brockville into a junior officers training centre will involve the construction of something like twenty-one buildings. At the western training centre, which is really not an officers training centre, at Red Deer, there will have to be a conversion of an existing reserve training centre to provide an advanced centre for the army service corps. This will involve the construction of eleven buildings.
Further, with regard to activities in Canada, we have had very much in mind, as 'I intimated when I spoke to the house at the last session, the necessity for the army doing everything it possibly can to avoid a drain on industry with respect to skilled men. I said then, and I repeat now, that we are anxious that the militia training under the National Resources Mobilization Act should not interfere unduly with industry. Second, we are prepared to assist by giving leave to men who are in the army and have special training and are needed in war industry. Third, we wanted to be on our own as much as possible by training our own men in connection with the motorized and mechanized corps. An army trades school is being started on May 1 where about 2,000 men can be trained at a time. The actual course will take from three to six months. This will not interfere with the courses in the civil technical institutions. We shall be training our own tradesmen. In addition, there is a diesel engine course being oonducted at the Dominion Engineering company. I wish it understood that I am not mixing this up with what is being done by the Department of Labour.

As hon. members know, that department is fostering the organization of plant schools in different industries. These schools are being used for vocational training in connection with war industries. The department has, I think, used, in whole or in part, the facilities of the youth training plan, and has mapped out a rather comprehensive system of technical training right across Canada for the purpose of meeting the necessities of our war situation.

I will conclude by recalling that the money which is asked for here, and which, as the Minister of Finance has indicated, amounts to something like 8660,000,000, is for an army programme which is very, very heavy in its implications. If the programme is carried out as envisaged, we shall have overseas a corps of three divisions, corps troops aggregating many thousands more; we shall have an army tank brigade; and we shall have an army division-extremely expensive, if I may use that expression in terms of dollars, as also is the army tank brigade-we have troops in Iceland, Newfoundland and the West Indies, and we shall have in this country the troops for our Canadian defence services, coast defence, guards and internment camps, mobile troops for operations, and in addition to these we have the bases and the organizations and the establishments for recruiting and equipping and training reinforcements and supplying other formations which may be needed from time to time. It is a big undertaking; and, as head of the branch of the department which has particularly to do with the army, I realize the responsibility one has in asking that this large sum of money be voted.

My hon. friend means
by "seniority," I suppose, which unit has been formed the longest, having regard to the history of the unit. I cannot say that seniority is follov'ed absolutely, but I can assure my hon. friend that it is taken into consideration. This is a wide-open invitation, but if any hon. member feels that there is any unit which, because of its military efficiency, he wants to bring to my attention as desirable to be raised as a unit, as a whole, I shall be very glad to see him, talk the matter over with him and put it before the officers. The ground on which units are picked is, I really believe, that of efficiency. I am certain that there has never been a single case which has come to my attention of a unit having been selected on any other ground than that the officers concerned believed it was the unit which could most efficiently and properly serve the purpose which was suggested for it. If there is any case where two units have an equal chance, and my hon. friends bring the matter to my attention, I will see that the officers consider the matter.
I was saying that there is the army programme for 1941 as we see it. An army programme these days has to be taken, as my colleague the Minister of Finance has said, on an "if, as and when" basis, because, sitting here to-night, we have no idea what is ahead of us in the next year. We are trying to plan so that any reasonable exigency can be met. We have had to make plans in the light of the best information we could get, and to get that information we have gone where we believed the information was most likely to be correct. We have made the plan. We are trying to lay the foundations solidly. The responsibilities are very great in their extent having regard to man-power, materials and money. I came home feeling that there was need for these units and therefore recommended them to my colleagues, and they have accepted the recommendation. So much for the overseas programme. In addition, we have, outside Canada, our troops in Iceland. Newfoundland and the Caribbean.
In Canada, as indicated, there are about
102,000	on the reserve, apart from recruits under the National Resources Mobilization Act. In addition to that, we have in Canada at the moment something over 100,000 in the active service force. As hon. members will see, there will be some change in that figure
War Appropriation Bill

when the formations to which I have referred go overseas; but we have a very heavy army programme. In that connection we have had to build establishments to provide for the housing since April, 1940,, less than a year ago, of nearly 100,000 men altogether. We have provided for the officer training centres of which I have spoken. We have provided for additional coast defence construction, and there is more now under way. We have provided over 2,000 beds in all in various hospitals. We have provided and are providing at the present time for the housing and maintenance of motor transport vehicles. There are twenty-two storage buildings which will house about 2,000 vehicles. We have in immediate prospect additional magazines, additional coast defence work and additional batteries, and we are also providing an army training school at Hamilton. I have given a very general indication of our programme.
My last word will be to my hon. friend who spoke before I did. This year we have not only a programme in the way of materials and money, but a programme which requires that we keep up the morale both of the men in the army and of Canadians at large. I really do not know of anything that is more important in this war than morale. Regardless of what may pass across this floor, I do hope, I wish to believe, that we are all one in the endeavour to see to it that the men who are in uniform are encouraged and heartened and that they have explained to them why this war is so different from the last. It should be explained to the people of the country why we have not the glamour, the music, the flags and all the things which were so common then.
We are having the regulation of man-power, the regulation of money, the regulation of materials, the regulation even of food, the regulation of everything in these days in an endeavour to make the fight tell and to achieve victory. It means that it is quite different from going ahead and spending and saying, "Let the morrow take care of itself." We are tiying to emerge successfully from the war without having our economy completely shattered.
It is a hard thing to do. It is hard for the people of the country, hard for the men in the ranks and for the officers themselves to keep going, without the excitement of actual warfare, which always, though it brings its injuries, its wounds and its deaths, has at the same time some excitement about it. I for one have felt that it was almost harder, in the absence of activity, to keep the armed

forces in the Shape in which they should be than if casualties, a great many of them, were taking place.
There is that difficulty, and I do ask members of this house and the public generally to help to look after the men in our armed forces and to see that they understand the situation.
We try to see that personal visits are paid to camps and, that everything possible is done to show that we have an interest in our soldiers. I wish to pay a special tribute to the auxiliary services-who by the way are putting on a campaign in a week or two-comprising the Young Men's Christian Association, the Knights of Columbus, the Salvation Army and the Canadian Legion, who are doing magnificent work all through the camps in Canada, in order to keep up the morale of the men, and doing the same thing as well under bombing conditions in England. I believe that job of helping to keep up the morale, both of the soldier and of the civilian, at this time, is about as great and important a task as men could undertake, and it is being done well.
There is the general outline for the army. As regards the overseas forces, I have indicated what is being done. In this country men are training constantly to furnish re-enforcements-and one would not believe what a large number of reenforcements we have to furnish even when conditions are comparatively static. If the time comes when there is so-called glamour, when there is the activity of warfare, demands upon the country for reenforcements will certainly try us to the utmost.
As regards this matter of morale, nothing could be finer than the example which I saw overseas of the men and women and children of the islands of Great Britain. It has almost become trite, but it can never be trite, to comment upon the way in which these people, day after day, stand up and take it-the nonchalance, almost, with which they go about their daily work in the face of constant danger; the way in which they set about repairing damage which is done, just as if it were an every day occurrence; the way in which they show their determination, not only by their indifference but by their active preparations for what they believe is coming, namely, invasion. All this is something which would inspire any man or woman and is a great challenge to us all.
We have a lot to be thankful for in this country, and very little to grouse about after all; and I do feel that the best way for us to get hold of the situation, the best way for us to cultivate the spirit and the morale which is necessary to win the war, is to look

War Appropriation Bill
across the seas to those people in. Great Britain and to think of what they are undergoing every day and night, yet remaining indomitable and doughty under the leadership of that valiant man, Mr. Churchill, whom I had the pleasure of meeting on a number of occasions-their faces towards the sun, their chins in the air. Nothing finer could be said to show their unconquerable spirit than that characteristic expression of theirs, "We can take it."
I think we can take it in this country if it comes to bearing the grimness and drabness of the absence of active warfare. I think we can take it in this country if it comes to paying taxes. There is no question about the people of this country being prepared to do anything they are asked so long as it will help to win the war. It has been a great heartener to me to find how the programme which has been announced has been accepted by the Canadian people, even though they know it is a very heavy one.
So, Mr. Chairman, with that very brief review I invite hon. members to ask any

I am glad my hon. friend has brought that up. I thought the information in connection with that point might be of interest to the committee. I had to look it up on one occasion, and I came across information which I believed would be of interest at this time. Away back in 1866 Viscount Monck in a dispatch to Lord Carnarvon, discussing the state of loyalty or otherwise of the provinces, suggested that it might be a good thing to found a Canadian order of chivalry. I should like to quote:
The want of the material in a new country for creating an hereditary aristocracy is one of the great difficulties in the way of applying the institutions of the British constitution to our colonies, and yet, without this or some substitute for it, we are in fact training up the minds of our colonists not to the ideas of monarchy but of republicanisms.
Then he goes on to discuss the whole matter, and concludes:
The plan which I would suggest for your lordship's consideration to meet the want to which I have referred would be the institution

War Appropriation Bill
of an order of knighthood for British North America on the model of the Order of the Star of India, to be called "the Order of St. Lawrence."
This matter was still further discussed no longer ago than during the course of the last war. Some of my hon. friends will recollect that there was in England a sub-militia council set up under the jurisdiction of the minister of militia of that day, Sir Sam Hughes. The members of that council were:
Major-General J. W. Carson,
Major-General J. C. MacDougall, C.M.G.,
Brigadier-General F. S. Meighen,
Colonel George P. Murphy,
Colonel Frank A. Reid,
Lieutenant-Colonel James G. Ross,
Major G. D. Oulster, Secretary.
Colonel McRae appears to have been a member of it at one time, also.
We also find here a minute from the meeting of the acting sub-militia council for overseas Canadians, held at Cleveland House, St. James square, London, on September 8, 1916. It reads:
Correspondence in connection with creating a Canadian order along the lines of the Order of the Star of India was brought up and discussed at the meeting, and it was moved by General Carson and seconded by General MacDougall that General Carson should write the Hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence, Canada, stating that the sub-militia council would recommend that he, the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence, consider the question of creating a Canadian order after the style of "The Star of India" and with just as strict regulations and rules. This order to be known as "The Order of the Beaver and Maple Leaf" or, "The Star of Canada."
Therefore I am glad my hon. friend gave me an opportunity to put on Hansard what has happened before with respect to the desirability of establishing in Canada an order of chivalry. I have not any doubt whatsoever but that means will be found to reward gallantly while in the face of the enemy, or in the course of active duty. With regard to the matter as to whether or not Canada should recommend to his majesty that we have orders of chivalry, I must say that I believe that this is a matter of higher policy to be settled probably in this house.

I am not competent to speak upon the matter raised by the hon. member for Shel-bume-Yarmouth-Clare. He referred to ships built partly of steel and partly of wood, and he states it is practicable to build this type of ship. If that is the case, then here is one way whereby ships can be built in large numbers on both our east and west coasts. There timber is available. My leader referred to a rolling mill in Nova Scotia which is not now in use. I assume this is due to the fact that all the steel production is under contract to the British government and is being shipped there just as rapidly as it is produced.
I do not know whether the Nova Scotia Steel company is able to obtain all the iron ore they require from Bell island, Newfoundland. I have been at Bell island and have seen how they take out iron ore from under the sea. They have good equipment for loading and are able to turn out many thousands of tons. If there is not sufficient iron ore available from this point, there are said to be ample supplies in the Hamilton river district in the Labrador. These are some of the best
War Appropriation Bill

deposits to be found in the world but they are still undeveloped. If the war continues for years, as it may, it may be found necessary to reopen the plate mill in Nova Scotia. If there is not sufficient ore available from Bell island, I would advise the government to consider obtaining supplies from the Hamilton river deposits.
Something has been said about building ships on both east and west coasts and numerous references have been made to Ontario. I see no reason for conflict between the east and the west and Ontario. We are nine provinces all united to do our best for Canada, and through Canada for the empire. It is quite true that steel plate is rolled only in Ontario, in one mill in the city of Hamilton. That mill has two large rolls and it is able to turn out steel in large quantities. I take pride-perhaps I should not-in the fact that in 1930 or 1931 I advocated in this bouse a duty on steel above 40 inches. This was to encourage the Hamilton mill to roll steel up to 78 inches. I believe the government of the day did protect steel up to 66 inches, and the Hamilton mill itself undertook bo roll up to 78 inches. Later on, I believe they considered rolling up bo 120 inches.
I am sure the fact that this steel is rolled in Hamilton has been of great help in our shipbuilding programme. There will soon be another mill opened in Hamilton, I believe in May. This mill will roll 40 inch plate, but this is the material used in constructing the smaller steel ships such as corvettes and so on. The minister has announced that some eighteen or twenty cargo ships are to be built in Canada, and then we have the statement in the press to-day that twenty-nine cargo ships were sunk in a week. I am convinced that this government should undertake to build, not eighteen cargo ships but 100 or 200. If the war lasts, as it apparently will, it will be imperative that we have ships. So far, the shipyards in England have not been destroyed. Most of them are located on the Clyde, Humber and Tyne, in the south of Scotland and the north of England. Perhaps it has been difficult for planes to fly that far with a heavy enough load, but it will be a sad day when they are able to do so and perhaps destroy these shipbuilding yards. Therefore it is all the more imperative that Canada should get into the shipbuilding business of both coasts. There are shipyards at Vancouver. Much of the steel used in these yards is shipped from Chicago, the plate rolled in Ontario being used there, too, and elsewhere. When the new Hamilton mill is in operation, I assume that a lot of plate produced there will be shipped to Vancouver.
IMr. MacNicol.]

I should have said
British Columbia, because there are shipbuilding facilities at New Westminster and Burrard. The government should consider what has been said by hon. members for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as well as by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Efforts should be made to build ocean cargo ships in both the east and the west. I might be asked, "Why not Ontario?" I do not believe that ocean cargo ships can be built economically in Ontario, and I have never advocated anything which was not economically sound. During the great war I understand a number of cargo ships were built in the vicinity of Detroit, then taken apart, shipped overland and reassembled, I believe in Florida. That would not be economical. If the government is planning to build cargo ships, they should be built in the east and the west. These ships can be built there and these provinces should be given something. I am not at all in accord with the idea of concentrating everything in one part of Canada.
I think the Ontario industrialist deserves unstinted praise for what he has done in this war by way of providing plants to build the equipment required in these ships as well as to produce other war munitions. Engines for ships are being built mainly in Montreal. At the present time the government is building three types of ships for war purposes, and it is now contemplating constructing ocean cargo boats. I repeat that these ocean cargo boats should be built on the Atlantic coast and on the Pacific coast. At least part of the steel will be rolled in Ontario and a lot of the other equipment can be provided by that province. In Ontario, as well as in other parts of Canada, the government is building fast power boats to provide protection against submarines and for other purposes. Quite a number of these will be built in the towns of Muskoka. Some will be built, I believe, on the western coast, at Prince Rupert and other centres, and perhaps some on the eastern coast. These are power boats, I understand, about 110 to 115 feet long.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is some development at Owen Sound, is there not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
These power boats go very fast. Then, in Ontario we are building corvettes and mine-sweepers. I have made a careful investigation in connection with minesweepers. Although the Minister of Munitions and Supply is not in his seat-he is working about twenty-four hours a day, doing several men's jobs, and we cannot expect him

War Appropriation Bill
to be here every minute-no doubt he will read what I am going to say and will, I believe, appreciate that for the building of mine-sweepers, steel is rolled about 54 and 56 inches wide, but upon arrival at the minesweeper plant it has to be sheared to 51 inches. I would suggest that if it is necessary that the government ship mine-sweeper steel, which is for the sides of the ships, east and west, it be sheared to the right length and width right in Ontario, because the extra freight is a big item to-day, and every possible dollar should be saved in construction and equipment. This is an all-out war. Not only will it take all our man-power, but it will take all our money besides.
I am glad to see that the Minister of Munitions and Supply is coming into the chamber. I have said, that I had not expected him to be here because he is doing so many men's jdbs, and he cannot be here all the time, but I am pleased that he has come in to hear something which I have been thinking. Even in the building of cargo ships, but more particularly in the building of corvettes and mine-sweepers, if the plates were shaped and drilled according to templets instead of one at a time, if the government would say to a particular producer of ships, "we want you to erect fifty corvettes and fifty minesweepers'. that would mean that in each case a large number of plates for the sides of these ships could be produced much more rapidly than is possible with only small contracts. I know, because I was for years in the boiler business, manufacturing boilers using steel of large dimensions, and in my time the individual plates for six boilers would be punched and drilled at the same time, very rapidly, and another six put on the same machines and so drilled. Perhaps 200 holes for rivets, more or less depending on the size of the plate, were made in this manner.
What I have seen of present production is not being carried on in that way, and I thought that in the reshaping of the minister's programme, as will probably be done when it is realized that the war will last for years, the minister should say to some one of these builders, "here is an order for fifty corvettes," or, "here is an order for fifty mine-sweepers," so that the producers could make them for less money than would be possible if they had just a few orders; they could so organize their production as to manufacture plate for the sides in multiple production. It could be done.
In like manner if, instead of a long time being taken to bend and shape the plate around, they could make the templets and the dies to produce the plate also bent in shape, as is desirable for multiple and rapid construction, considerable economies could be effected, but we could not expect them to do that if their plant received an order for not more than four or five ships; it would cost too much to make the necessary templets and dies. I have confidence in the minister to this extent, that if and when he decides to build ships in large numbers he, understanding thoroughly the production of these appliances, might induce the companies to manufacture under conditions of multiple production, as was done in the last war. In the United States ships were turned out almost as rapidly as sardine cans. All plates for particular parts of ships were made at the same time for scores and scores of vessels; and we shall have to get into that system too. That would apply to corvettes and mine-sweepers, and to other equipment.
I have heard some people condemn our shipbuilding programme as being behind schedule. I have heard the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services say that it is ahead of schedule. I doubt if it is, but I am not going to blame either minister on that account, because everybody who studies these things knows that after the battle of the Mediterranean it was necessary to make considerable changes in the designs of ship fittings.
The dropping of bombs by the German Stuka dive bombers alongside the ships rocked the Illustrious as though it were a cork in the water, and the effects were discovered when it reached Malta. It was learned on examination of the Illustrious, and by the effects of bombing on the cruiser which was sunk by the British themselves, what would have to be done in future interior construction. I will not elaborate on the effects of the bombs which had dropped all round the ship as well as on top of it; but after these ships had been shaken as the Illustrious was shaken by these tremendous bombs, engineers made a careful survey and found it necessary to recommend some changes in interior construction. I am not going to ask the minister to say that such changes have been carried out here, but if there has been any delay in the production of corvettes-I know that some have been launched-or of mine-sweepers, perhaps that is one of the reasons. Such a reason would carry weight with me. I am not going to condemn the minister if production has been retarded because so many things have entered into the construction of ships for the sea since the war broke out, and since engineers have surveyed what has happened to some of the boats which have been exposed to enemy action, changes have had to be made. I am sure I am right in that regard.

War Appropriation Bill

But, changes having been made, production should proceed rapidly. I have not any doubt that in due course, with yards organized east and west, as well as in Ontario, production will increase. In any event, this house, I am sure, will support the government, because party politics is not worth a fig in war time. It is an all-out war; we here are all Canadians and all British to assist in fighting this war; and if 100 million dollars are required to equip the yards and the mills. I for one, and I am sure everyone else, would be glad to vote whatever is required, because if we win the war	we	save	all, and if we lose	thewar we lose	all.	We	might better lose a	lot
in winning the war.
I think that is about all I have to say, except for one thing of which I have spoken before; I should like to say a word about it to the minister again. Adjacent to Windsor there is a big plant. It has its blast furnaces; there is a railway from the river to the plant, and there is	a	canal	alongside built by	thecompany up	to	the steel plant. It is a huge
plant; I have been in it and so have others. But it is now being used for a purpose for which it was not built; it is being used in part for small affairs connected, I believe, with machine guns of one kind or another. It is essentially a steel plant and a shipbuilding plant. I am not able to say who owns it, but I believe it is the Walkerville company-

Dominion Steel. The hon. member is referring to the Ojibway plant?

speechtext:
Yes, a huge plant with a great deal of good machinery in it which should not be used for the purpose for which it is now being used. It has its own blast furnaces. They may need repairing, because I do not know whether they are up-to-date blast furnaces. Changes are necessary from time to time. But I cannot see why that plant is not in operation for the purpose for which it was erected.
I hate to throw any further load upon the shoulders of the minister. He is already burdened with machine guns, aeroplanes and everything else; he is carrying a terrific, tremendous load, and I wish to help him instead of adding still further to his burden. I desire, however, to impress upon him the importance of building ships. I do not want to say it is the one vital problem before us, but we simply must get troops to England; we must transport vast supplies of war munitions-and as a matter of fact we are shipping trainloads of materials now. On Sunday I saw a trainload of shell lathes which

would turn out nine-inch shells in either four or eight minutes. I believe the time is four minutes. A fourteen-year-old girl can. turn out a nine-inch shell in that space of time on these new, high-powered, high-speed shell lathes, which had so much to do with saving England. Shell lathes are made in Toronto and elsewhere, but the one I have in mind was made in Toronto. I said a trainload; I believe there were ten cars of these great machines ready for export, and it is essential that they should reach England. It is essential that our guns and everything else, our pork, our wheat, our farm products, should reach England; and they must go in ships. In my judgment, therefore, the minister will find shortly that the whole shipbuilding programme will have to be revamped with the objective of perhaps making it one hundred times bigger than it is to-day. Yards for building ocean cargo ships at Saint John, Halifax, Sydney and anywhere else where plants of that kind can be erected-someone says Miramichi, but I presume any ships built there would have to be wooden ships- Vancouver, Burrard, Victoria and elsewhere, will be necessary to develop the plan. It is a big programme.
I want to do what I can to assist the minister, because we must win the war. All this material is urgently required, considering the rate of losses, twenty-nine ships last week. How long can we stand it? We could equip the country to build twenty-nine ships a month. They did in the United States in the last war, and perhaps we could do it now if we all got together and built the necessary plants.
I am sorry for the Minister of Finance, who has to endeavour to raise so much money, but Canadians will support him in raising whatever is demanded. There are no more loyal British subjects in the world than Canadians. They are all-out in this war and will go the limit; and, as far as I am concerned, I would sooner give all I have, whatever little it may be, for the honour of my country, and die if need be, than lose the war.

speechtext: It is always a delight for me to hear my hon. friend the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) discuss matters of this kind. He is a well informed and practical man and he adopts a kindly tone. Unfortunately, I did not hear his opening remarks. I can hardly credit it, but someone told me that he made a slight slip when he compared tons of steel with tons of ships.

Oh, no, I did not say that. I said that we are at present producing in Canada approximately 1,500 tons of pig-iron a day, produced by the Algoma plant,

the Helen mountain mines, and I pointed out that there are being sunk on the ocean ships representing a displacement of 150,000 tons a week, not a day. The article this morning said about 148,000 tons, but I said 150,000 had been sunk during the past week, so as to give round figures. With regard to building ships to take the place of those that are sunk, assuming that the ships themselves aggregated

speechtext:
A deadweight ton, of course, does not take a ton of steel, but much less, depending upon the size of the boat. I just wanted to call attention to that fact, because 1 found my hon. friends equating tons of steel with tons of ships, and I am sure my hon. friend did not mean to imply that that would be done. He must, however, realize the position of the Department of Munitions and Supply when he speaks of an unlimited number of corvettes. We build to fill orders, and in the matter of corvettes, of course, I suppose the number of crews that can be furnished is the determining factor. We cannot go full-out on an unlimited number of corvettes unless either our navy or the British navy indicate that they require them. What we are going full-out on is the matter of cargo ships. They are a different story, and we can go full-out there and in the meantime fill all orders, having substantial orders for corvettes and mine-sweepers.
Our policy there is to plan a long-range programme for corvettes and mine-sweepers for the lakes, for the reason that we cannot get a cargo ship out of the lakes, and therefore these shipyards are not available as far as the larger boats go. We are, however, directing our efforts more and more to get a large boat programme for the lower St. Lawrence and coast yards. We intend to press that as far as we can. The difficulty then becomes a matter of man-power. It is not difficult to organize a shipyard. The capital cost is not large in comparison with output, but the matter of getting a skilled crew to man the shipyard is extremely difficult, and we were warned in England not to undertake that if it meant stripping other yards to get personnel, which is what it would mean in Canada to-day.
We are approaching cautiously, studying the problem to see how far the structural steel companies can assist us, and I can say that we are advancing in that just as rapidly as prudence will permit.
As far as the Ojibway plant of the Dosco company is concerned, that has been studied carefully. The blast furnaces are old. They have been out of use for about twenty years, 14873-92}
and it was found that we would be better off if the furnaces were not there. They would have to be completely rebuilt. The capital cost is very high and the time involved is an important factor. The best estimate we have had on time is about two years.
It is a question how far we should go in extending the steel capacity of Canada. We had at the beginning of the war a theoretical capacity of about 2,200,000 tons of steel per annum. We have expanded that by 500,000 tons. Whether we should go further than that, I think is a matter that deserves careful study. We normally import in good times about one million tons of steel from outside Canada. From a study of the situation it would appear that for our present programme of war requirements we shall not require to import more than a million tons of steel a year in addition to our capacity. That may vary from time to time, but that is the present forecast. To arrive at that figure we planned a curtailment of the domestic use of steel, and we have been enforcing that curtailment for the last six or eight months. I see no harm in curtailing the domestic use of steel; in fact, I think our programme will more and more tend towards curtailment of domestic use of all materials that go into munitions of war; that is a logical development in putting the country on an all-out war basis.
We have determined that we are protected for one million tons per annum of steel from outside Canada. How far we should go in disorganizing the normal economy of Canada by expanding the steel industry beyond the point we have reached is a matter that is receiving careful study. There is a good deal of sound opinion in the direction of not expanding further at the moment.
As I said, however, we are going all-out on ships. We are going to build as many ships as we can build by reasonably sound economic methods. We are studying mass production methods in use elsewhere. They were developed to a small extent late in the last war at Hog island, but it did not continue long enough to bring the mass production theory into practice. It is being attempted again in this war and we are watching the procedure carefully to see to what extent it can be adapted to Canadian use.
I make these few remarks to indicate to the hon. member for Davenport that we are proceeding along the lines he suggested.
