speechtext:
I wish to direct the attention of the committee to something of a quite different nature. We have for some little time been dealing with moneys heretofore spent. I want to deal with a question which I think may be described as one of present waste, serious waste and extravagance. I refer to one of the government's companies. I do not desire to leave the committee in doubt for a moment, so I say that company is Allied War Supplies Corporation. I am starting a conversation which will perhaps be rather in the nature of question and answer.
I remind the committee that near Winnipeg there is just now being brought into being a very large cordite plant. The expenditure, as has been mentioned several times, is in the neighbourhood of $10,000,000. As I understand the situation, the contract for the building of that contract is let by Allied War Supplies Corporation, and then the plant is to be operated by another company which we call D.I.L., Defence Industries Limited. That company, I understand, is simply Canadian Industries Limited, organized for convenience under the name D.I.L. Convenience, I say, because they are doing quite a bit of contract work and it is easier to have all that work carried on by this separate company. I am not sure if I have that exactly correct, but I believe it is very close to it.
That large cordite plant will require a great deal of steam. To produce that steam will require a great deal of coal. When they invited tenders they let it be known that they would need about fifty thousand tons of coal a year. Apparently at that time they were considering all kinds of coal.
We have in western Canada a certain field known as the economic field in which lignite coal can be burned. Roughly speaking, I

believe it runs from Swift Current to Kenora. At any rate, whatever the area be, Winnipeg is certainly within it. No one would, I believe, suggest that Edmonton or Sudbury is. It is, as I understand it, a question of freight rates.
Allied War Supplies Corporation has had a number of prices submitted. It has apparently decided to take what it admits to be the more expensive kind of fuel rather than the less expensive kind. A variety of reasons have been given; I do not think any of their reasons are satisfactory, and they are not consistent one with another. I am not blaming the minister in this connection; I think most hon. members will agree that this way of handling government business is, generally speaking, pretty sound. At the present time, however, this organization is embarking upon a method of providing at that plant steam which will cost $100,000 or $200,000 more per annum than it should cost. There is no need to waste public money in that way. This organization is just as much a trustee of public moneys as is every member of this house, every member of the government and every other person engaged in our war effort. A very large part of the money to be provided under this legislation will be handled by this corporation, which I say is now embarking upon a wasteful plan of creating steam for that plant.
Perhaps I would not be quite so sure of this, were it not for the fact that they have given so many different explanations as to why they will not bum lignite coal. At one stage, for instance, they said the supply was not dependable. I talked with the engineer who made those recommendations. He boiled it down substantially to that one proposition, the dependability of supplies. Well, the one coal that they can get for about 75 cents a ton at the mine is only two hundred miles from Winnipeg, and there is rail connection by both railways. This engineer kept on talking about the dependability of supply, but he recognized and admitted that this coal could come in steadily, hour by hour and day by day. He tried to raise certain other objections against the use of lignite coal and then, after all that argument and after stating that he could not use lignite coal at all, he suggested the possibility of using 40 per cent of the cheaper coal. First, it was stated by this engineer and by other members of this corporation that they could not use this coal at all, that it was not a feasible proposition; but before very long they were saying they could use 40 per cent, and I understand that now they have increased that percentage substantially.
I might be willing to withdraw the first charge I made, that they were entering upon

War Appropriation Bill
this extravagance, if I could believe their statement that they are going to use a large percentage of lignite coal, but everything points to the fact that they are simply saying they are going to do this while they know full well the equipment they are putting in that plant will not permit them to do it. I charge that this organization, the creature of this parliament, is simply playing horse with the minister. These people are telling him they are going to do something which they really do not intend to do. I recall that this same organization undertook to install equipment in a large plant of the Winnipeg hydro for burning lignite coal. They have never burned an ounce of lignite from that day to this. They equipped our plant in Winnipeg for the burning of lignite coal, but they have never burned any of it, and they did that for the same purpose that I am protesting against now.
There has not been an important plant in that economic lignite area equipped in recent years to burn anything but lignite coal. No new equipment has gone into any plant except to burn this cheaper coal; but now in war time when taxes are heavy and are going to be still heavier, a creature of this government undertakes to do something in the more expensive rather than the less expensive way. I believe their plea now is that it is too late to change, that they have committed themselves. I do not think it is too late; I believe money can be saved if they will alter any decisions they have made heretofore. I should like to have on record any explanations there may be, and I want to serve notice that every undertaking given by this organization will be watched most carefully, not only every day of this year but every day they are out there. I do not believe they are going to do what they are promising. They are going to do what they originally intended to do; they are going to produce steam at a cost of $100,000 or 8200,000 greater than it should be. That is what they will do unless they are prevented.

speechtext:
Since D.I.L. and C.I.L. have been mentioned, perhaps I should explain the situation. I think the reason for the two companies will commend itself to the committee.
As hon. members know, firms engaged in the manufacture of explosives during the last war, such as du Pont, Hercules and perhaps Canadian Industries, were accused of profiteering. Those accusations became so numerous that they had quite an effect on the domestic business of these companies. Canadian Industries Limited, du Pont and the other companies which make explosives, also have very large peace-time businesses which, I
think, are conducted on excellent business lines and which, I believe, they have a right to segregate from their war work. Canadian Industries Limited wished to make their explosives experts available to the government's war effort, and wished to do a real war job; but at the same time they wished to keep their peace-time industry separate from that war work. As a result, they formed a separate company called Defence Industries Limited, which takes and executes all war contracts drawing on the technical skill of Canadian Industries Limited. In this way, all war profits are in the one company, Defence Industries Limited, where they are subject to taxation, to examination and to audit, and are entirely under the control of the government, while on the other hand C.I.L. keeps entirely to its peacetime pursuits.
I think that is quite commendable, and I should like to make sure that the committee does not draw any wrong inference from the fact that Defence Industries Limited, a new company, is handling the war work. I may say that we have engaged Defence Industries Limited as our experts on explosives. We have drawn on their technical skill to design and also bo operate explosive plants. Our explosives and chemical programme is, however, in the hands of Allied War Supplies Corporation, headed by Mr. Harold Crabtree, a chemical engineer with a wide business experience in Canada. He happens to be the president of the Canadian Manufacturers association, and a man in whom industry in Canada has a great deal of confidence. We have associated with him some seven or eight business executives, who also are highly respected in Canada for the efficiency of the operation for which they aTe responsible.

speechtext:
Serving
without remuneration?

speechtext:
Yes, all serving without
remuneration. Mr. Crabtree is giving his full time; in fact, I think he is giving about two days in one, and has been doing that since he received the appointment,
I believe the country will recognize the excellent work these men have been doing in working out our chemicals and explosives programme, which is a very large programme indeed. In the planning of the Winnipeg plant this company proceeded with Defence Industries Limited as their expert engineers to design the plant, as they have designed other explosives plants, two of which are now in operation. This is the third.
It was called to my attention some time ago that there was a strong feeling in Winnipeg that this plant should use lignite coal. I dropped a line to Mr. Crabtree, directing his
War Appropriation Bill

attention to the fact that lignite coal was being used to a great extent in Winnipeg for heating purposes in the larger plants, and asking him particularly to look into the situation to make sure that he was making a wise decision in providing the type of equipment for which he had provided, namely, an underfeed stoker. The lignite coal requires a different type of equipment. Mr. Crabtree wrote me on the subject, and later we had an interview in connection with it, on which occasion he brought the report of his engineers, estimated costs and other technical data. We spent sometime together going into that project. He pointed out that an explosives plant is built for operation only during war time. Of course there is no need for an explosives plant of that size in peace time, particularly as it is one of three plants, the other two being considerably larger than the one planned for Winnipeg. The question as to whether or not we were warranted in spending a considerable additional sum to put in equipment which would bum lignite coal efficiently, and only lignite coal, was studied by the engineers. They had to decide also as to whether the equipment would be disposable after the war. That is an important factor which must not be forgotten. This is large equipment, and so far lignite equipment of the size here indicated has never been installed in Canada. It is therefore unlikely that there would be a market for that type of equipment after the war. On the other hand, the underfeed stoker type is common in Canada, and probably would be marketable after its use in Winnipeg comes to an end.
Then the question as to the respective economies of the two coals was studied, and it was the considered opinion of Mr. Crabtree's engineers and of Mr. Crabtree, after making his own study of the matter, in the light of the reports he had received, that it would not be wise to go to the extra expense of putting in special equipment to burn lignite coal.
Mr. Crabtree believes that he would be able to bum a very high percentage of lignite coal in these boilers. I hope that is true, because we are finding it rather difficult to get supplies of bituminous coal from western Canada at the present time. The use of lignite coal at Winnipeg would have a balancing effect upon the coal situation in western Canada. Mr. Crabtree tells me that he will be able to use a considerable portion of lignite coal. He has studied the question, and I have a good deal of confidence in his statement in the matter.
All I can say to the committee is that having turned over the explosives and chemicals programme to Allied War Supplies Corporation, and having had ample demonstration

that they are able to handle that type of work, as demonstrated by the plants they have brought into operation prior to this date, I have not found anything in the situation which would warrant me as the responsible minister in reversing the decision arrived at by the corporation.

speechtext:
The minister has made two observations to which I shall refer. In the first place he turned his attention to the organizations known as C.I.L. and D.I.L. and explained that that was apparently good business practice, under the circumstances, adding that he did not want the committee to get off on the wrong foot. We might as well have that point settled immediately. So far as I am concerned I entirely agree with that. I did not intend to make any suggestion to the committee that there was anything improper in the manner of organizing. In fact, in introducing my remarks I said that the division had been made apparently for convenience.
Since, however, we have mentioned C.I.L. and D.I.L., I might add to what I have already said, that when C.I.L. was putting in its own plant, the Allied War Supplies Corporation was not in the picture at all. Rather it was putting in its own plant, for its own commercial purposes and, like every other organization in western Canada, it put in a plant for the purpose of burning lignite. It is situated at Neepawa, Manitoba, where they have their salt industry. Therefore, for commercial purposes that is what they did.
But this other corporation, the one that is the direct creature of the government and of parliament, is the organization which is doing what I have been describing. They may be using the C.I.L. personnel and they may not. Certainly they are not using it entirely. One man they are using, and who had been very active, is a man who comes from the organization that sells this kind of equipment. I was not trying to convince him, because I do not profess to have engineering knowledge. Let me say in passing that I do not want to see $100,000 or $200,000 wasted each year. I was not trying to convince him, nor do I believe I was able to convince him. But his remark was, "They might be able to convince some people, but they will never convince me." This man comes from the organization which sells the equipment.
The same man was in western Canada for a long time, and by reason of the development

War Appropriation Bill
of the practice of burning lignite coal he and his company withdrew from that territory, because they did not make the kind of equipment that would burn that coal. I do not know when the interviews took place to which the minister has referred. I do know that about eight or nine days ago Mr. Crabtree stated to a colleague of mine in this house that this question was still an open one, that they would approach it with open minds, and yet within thirty-six hours this man Abbott sat in a room in this House of Commons with that same colleague and me and told us that it was a closed book, that it had been closed for months. He said, "I do not think Mr. Crabtree would misrepresent it, but that book is a closed book and it has been closed." Those are my words; they are not the precise words used, but I think they give an accurate rendering of the conversation I had with him.
Reference has been made to two or three different kinds of equipment. The authority which I have for anything I may offer in the way of describing the equipment is not a person interested in making a sale in opposition to these people; it is our own fuel laboratory experts here. They tell me there are two diSerent ways of carrying coal into the furnace. One is to carry it in and sprinkle it on top, known as the "kicker" system. I do not profess to have any mechanical knowledge; I am simply trying to describe what I have been told, in words which make myself understood.
When the engineer finished talking to me I took the precaution of converting his statement into words such as I would use and asking him whether they covered the situation. When I talk to hon. members about equipment in the way I do, they will know the background for my statement. They will see how I came to get this particular description into my own mind. As I say, substantially there are two methods of putting coal into a firebox to be burned. One is the kicker system, and the other is the underfeed. The underfeed equipment is not suitable for burning lignite coal, and that is the system which these people put into the Winnipeg hydro. They have not burned an ounce of lignite coal. I might give a further authority for that proposition in the person of the engineer I told the committee about, Mr. Abbott. He is the man who has been behind this, who came to us from the company that makes this equipment. He agreed readily that underfeed equipment was not satisfactory for burning this coal.
As I say, I do not know when the conversation referred to by the minister took place, but I do know that I got this information
from the department of the government as far back as January 13. These people were stating that it was a closed book because Mr. W. H. Wharton of the Allied War Supplies had said so. I am not talking about the D.I.L.; I am talking about an organization which is a child of this government and which is supposed to have all this authority. This man said that they had ruled against lignite coal. In spite of that, I want to repeat that Mr. Crabtree stated only a short time ago that they would approach this matter with an open mind. When one runs into two propositions which are so completely contrary, it is enough to make one suspicious. When within thirty-six hours another man from the same organization says in eSect that it was a closed book, that it could not be approached with an open mind, one is justified in being doubly suspicious.
Before going any further, I should like to make this comment with reference to giving full authority to this organization. I agree that the right course has been taken in forming these companies in order to get the work of government decentralized. As soon as I saw the announcement by the government I felt that the right step had been taken, that it would afford a means of saving harassed and overworked ministers. No matter how vehement I may be at times, I think the government made a right move by turning over considerable responsibility to an organization of this kind. But there is a great difference between giving them considerable responsibility and completely abrogating in favour of them. No organization should be able to go out and spend the money of the people of Canada and not be subject to review. This sort of thing getting around the country is the worst possible thing one could have from the viewpoint of this department which is being so well administered by the minister of defence. Nothing in the world can hurt the idea of getting people to present their savings and being ready to accept taxes more than allowing it to be known that we have abrogated some function of government to certain commercial concerns. A number of fine gentlemen have been collected together to operate these organizations. With the exception of the one whom I have mentioned, I have no complaint to make about them, but they should not be considered as the government of this country.
